value: A political agitation in a town blocked a road in breach of a prohibitory order. Protesters damaged public buses, and one town bus had its seats set alight. Two buses carrying university students on an educational tour had been parked nearby. The bus carrying 47 female students was then approached by men who carried petrol in plastic cans. One man sprinkled petrol inside the bus through a window shutter while another sprinkled petrol through the second shutter, then a match was lit and thrown into the bus and it caught fire while students were still inside. The teachers on board pleaded with the men to stop. Students escaped through the front entrance, some stretched out through the shutters and were pulled out by male students, but three students could not escape and were burnt to death, and about twenty others received burn injuries. The driver and cleaner of the bus stated that two men on a motorcycle stopped beside the bus; one sprinkled petrol and both fled, the motorcycle engine having been kept running. Injured students and teachers identified the accused in a test identification parade held in jail and in court, with the identification process conducted by a Judicial Magistrate who prepared reports. Several initial investigators conducted the investigation in a charged atmosphere, after which the case was transferred to a specialised investigation unit. One accused was arrested later and gave a confessional statement. Post-mortem examinations were conducted on the three deceased students.

value: On a night in March 1996, the complainant and her daughter-in-law were sleeping in the complainant's house at about 11.30 PM. No adult male was in the house apart from children. The accused jumped over the front wall, broke the outside bulbs and ran away. Around 12.30 AM the accused returned by scaling the door and caught the daughter-in-law's hand. She raised an alarm and the complainant woke up, after which the accused ran away. The complainant's FIR statement and testimony described the incident this way. The daughter-in-law identified the accused and gave evidence of both visits. In cross-examination, the complainant and the daughter-in-law agreed the accused had not touched, teased or abused the complainant and had not gone towards or spoken to her. Both said the accused lived 15-16 houses away and the families were not on visiting terms. A defence witness, the former village sarpanch, said a quarrel over a water course with the complainant's son had turned into the complaint. The police investigated the complaint and submitted a report under Section 173 of the Code.

value: The complainant is a company that manufactures and sells industrial explosives and obtained ammonium nitrate, a major raw material, from a supplier company. Under a tripartite arrangement with the supplier and a coal company, the complainant was to pay an equivalent value to the coal company, which would supply coal to the supplier, and the supplier would supply ammonium nitrate to the complainant. The supplier supplied ammonium nitrate for some time, then stopped because of a breakdown of a gas compressor and financial difficulties. The supplier had earlier been declared a sick company, and its winding up was under consideration by the relevant authority. The complainant alleges that the accused, who were senior employees of the supplier, deliberately concealed this status and the supplier's large dues to other creditors. It alleges that this induced the complainant to pay about Rs. 4.20 crore to the coal company between September and November 2001, without receiving ammonium nitrate in return. The complaint also alleges collusion between the accused. The material relied on is the complaint and the averments in the complainant's civil suit plaint against the supplier.

value: The victim, a woman, lived on the first floor of a family house with her adult son; a relative of the accused lived on the ground floor with his wife. The accused, who lived in another city, was a regular visitor to the house. On the day of the incident the accused arrived by car at about 11.30 a.m. The ground-floor occupant's wife offered the accused a meal, and the accused said the accused would eat with the ground-floor occupant. Shortly afterwards the household maid heard screams from the victim's room. At about 2.30 p.m. the victim's son came to collect money and found the room locked from inside. He heard the accused talking on a telephone and asked the accused to open the door, which the accused refused. The ground-floor occupant also asked for the door to be opened, and the accused replied that the door would be opened only when police arrived. When police arrived, the accused opened the door and stated that the accused had killed the victim. The accused was holding a blood-stained sword, and the accused's clothing and hands were blood-stained. The victim was lying on a bed, her body smeared with blood. The sword, its sheath, blood-stained bedsheets and a gold bala were seized, and the accused's clothing and hand washings were taken. The post-mortem examination recorded seventeen injuries, all but three of them incised wounds that could be caused by a sharp-edged weapon such as a sword. The accused gave no explanation for being in the locked room or for holding the blood-stained sword. An injury report on the accused recorded an examination time of 11.30 a.m., which the accused relied on to suggest being in police custody at that time; its author was not examined as a witness.

value: A married woman aged about 24 was found dead in the bedroom of her matrimonial home about three years after her marriage. Her death was caused by strangulation and burning. The victim's father alleged that after about six months of marriage the accused, her husband and mother-in-law, repeatedly demanded a Maruti car as dowry. He stated that the victim told him of being tortured and maltreated for non-fulfilment of the demand, both over the telephone and on visits to her parental home. About three months before the death, the father and a relative went to the matrimonial home to try to resolve the matter. They were humiliated and told not to return without meeting the demand. The post mortem by a panel of three doctors recorded a ligature mark about 31 by 7 centimetres around the neck, a half-burnt cloth with a knot tied around the neck, superficial to deep burns over the body, and a smell of kerosene. The cause of death was recorded as suffocation with shock from strangulation with simultaneous ante-mortem burns. Investigators recovered blood and a bloodstained bindi from a balcony outside the room, broken bangles inside the room, and a burnt cordless phone and burnt wire stuck with the body. The body was found in a corner of the bedroom. The accused claimed the death was suicide. The mother-in-law lodged a police report stating that the victim had committed suicide. Both accused were absconding for some days before the husband surrendered and then the mother-in-law did.

value: On the night of 6 January 2000, the accused was on security duty as guard commander at a technical battery area of an army unit, armed with a 7.62 mm self-loading rifle and 20 cartridges. Following a report that stones had been thrown at the guard hut, the security junior commissioned officer ordered a Quick Reaction Team to be summoned. The team reached the guard hut at about 10.30 p.m., where the vehicle was challenged by the sentry on duty. Team members got out and moved to the right and left to locate the person who had thrown the stones. The accused ran toward one team member, the victim, while another team member followed and warned that the person being run toward was a member of the Quick Reaction Team and should not be fired upon. Despite this warning, the accused fired three shots from a distance of 8 to 10 feet, killing the victim at the spot. The accused was quickly apprehended by a sentry and the security junior commissioned officer. When questioned about what had been done, the accused replied 'MAINE JO KARNA THA KAR DIYA'. Evidence presented included the testimony of several army personnel who witnessed the shooting, post-mortem observations regarding the firing distance, and empty cartridge cases lifted from the site that matched the issued weapon.

value: The victim had a long-running rivalry with the accused, arising from competition for a liquor shop licence near a railway station and later incidents, including an assault, a theft complaint and an earlier attempt on the victim's life a few months before the shooting. On the day in question, the victim was returning on a cycle from a government food-grain depot with two companions, who were about 15 to 20 paces behind him. The accused arrived on a motorcycle carrying a double-barrelled gun. On seeing the accused, the victim left his cycle and ran toward a neighbouring plot. A single shot was fired, and the victim fell with gunshot injuries. The accused fled, leaving the motorcycle at the scene. The two companions stated that they did not chase the accused. The victim was taken by bullock cart to a hospital, and a complaint was lodged at the police station. A magistrate recorded the victim's statement at the hospital, noting the victim was in a serious condition. A doctor examined the victim and found multiple gunshot wounds on the chest, abdomen, arms, hand and thigh, and a further wound on the neck. The victim died later that night. A post-mortem examination found multiple gunshot wounds of entry, consistent with the medical examination. Investigators collected the motorcycle, a basket of goods, blood-stained and unstained earth, wads from the spot, and blood-stained clothing of the victim.

value: On the morning of 29 September 1991, the victim went to his field to harvest a bajra crop with his wife and son. A group of persons arrived armed with an axe, sickles, sticks and a jailli. They raised a challenge that they would teach the victim a lesson for interfering in a land purchase. One attacker struck the victim's knee with an axe, others felled him and beat him with sticks and sickles, and the attackers also struck the victim's wife and son when they tried to intervene. A bystander who intervened was struck on the knee. Attracted by an alarm, other villagers arrived. The attackers then lifted the injured victim and carried him to a tubewell belonging to one of the group, where he was left bleeding, and the attackers ran away. The victim's son informed the village, and the injured were taken to a Primary Health Centre. The victim was referred to a civil hospital, where he died the same afternoon. The victim's wife and son were discharged after medical examination. The wife's statement was recorded in the evening and a first information report was registered that night. The post-mortem report recorded 26 injuries, including fractures of both forearm bones, both leg bones and a foot, fractures of the ninth and tenth right ribs that lacerated the liver, and the doctor opined that the injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. Investigating officers visited the field and the tubewell, collected chappals, a broken rapri, a rope, a blood-stained matchbox and blood-stained earth, and prepared site plans which matched the revenue official's plan. value: On the afternoon of 25 May 1999, around 12.30 p.m., the victim was at a tyre shop. The prosecution case was that about ten to twelve armed persons, carrying gupties, swords, knives and gandasas, surrounded the victim and attacked him, inflicting multiple incised and penetrating wounds to the head, face, neck, chest, abdomen, back and arms. The report lodged by the victim's brother was registered as an FIR and investigated. A charge-sheet was filed against two named persons, and investigation against others was kept pending. The shop owner testified that the victim came alone on a motorcycle to repay a debt and talked with him for about 15 minutes. He then went to the basement, and on returning found the victim gone. He later found the victim dead in a pool of blood in the street. Police removed the body within five to ten minutes. He said the victim's brother arrived about ten minutes after the removal, and that he had given no names because he had not seen the attack. Three police witnesses, including the constable and driver who lifted the body, stated that the victim's brother and two other alleged eyewitnesses were not present. The post-mortem report recorded excessive haemorrhage from injuries to the right lung and liver as the cause of death. Three named eyewitnesses testified that they saw the attack.

value: The victim and two companions were travelling to a court hearing by bus, got off at about 11:15 a.m. at a bus stand, and walked towards the courts. value: On 22 March 1998, the accused reported to a section in-charge that the victim and another soldier had abused him with a derogatory word. The section in-charge questioned them and they denied it. The accused also reported a heated exchange with the victim the previous night. Later that day the victim returned to the barrack after lunch and lay on his cot near the door. Another soldier, who had also just returned to the barrack, saw the accused approach the door wearing a half T-shirt and a lungi. The accused took a knife hidden in the lungi and stabbed the sleeping victim once on the right side of the chest. The eyewitness shouted at the accused and others gathered; the accused was separated from the victim, who was taken to hospital and later died. The regimental medical officer testified that the only external injury was the knife wound. The knife, made of iron with a sharp edge, was among the evidence collected. The victim had also given a dying declaration to another soldier, who testified. The eyewitness could not link the stabbing to the earlier abuse or argument. Timing evidence showed about 40 to 45 minutes between the accused's return from the higher officer's office and the stabbing, during which the accused and the victim were in the same barrack without any conversation.

value: The victim was clearing a plot of land in front of a cattle shed where cattle grazed, while a title suit over the plot was pending between the victim's side and the accused. That accused went to a house and returned with a gun, accompanied by other accused carrying spears, farsa and lathis. Abusive language was exchanged with the victim. The victim's uncle went to the police station and a first information report was recorded the same afternoon. value: The victim had a dispute with his brother over a residential house. On the day of the incident, the victim, his wife and his daughters were at home. A group of accused persons, including the victim's brother and other family members, entered the house and attacked the victim and his family. One accused was holding an iron rod and struck the victim a blow on the head and left ear. Other accused beat the victim with lathis on his back, hips and other parts of the body, and the victim's wife and daughter were also injured with lathi blows. The accused then ran away, threatening to kill the family on the next opportunity. The injured were taken to a government hospital. The attending doctor was asked whether the victim was fit to make a statement and certified that he was. A police head constable then recorded the victim's statement, which the doctor endorsed after confirming its accuracy and which the victim's children also signed. The statement described the role of each accused and formed the basis of the first information report. The medico-legal examination recorded multiple lacerated wounds, contusions and abrasions, including a lacerated wound on the right side of the head. The victim's condition later worsened and he was transferred to another hospital, where he died about a week after the incident. The post-mortem was conducted by a doctor. Investigators recovered lathis and dandas following disclosure statements by accused persons. At trial, the victim's wife and daughter did not support the prosecution account, and the victim's son and daughter were not examined as witnesses.

value: The victim was asked by the accused and two family members to reap the accused's family's crop the next day. The accused and one companion were armed with lathis and the third was armed with a rifle. They asked the victim why he had not gone to reap the crop. After the victim repeated his refusal, the accused and a companion began abusing and beating the victim's son with lathis. Other family members, including the victim's mother, sister, another son and a relative, rushed to protect the son and were also struck with lathis and injured. The victim then intervened. One of the companions was told to shoot the victim, and fired a shot that struck the victim in the stomach, causing death. The same person also fired at the victim's son but the pellets missed him. Pellets injured another son and the daughter. After the shooting, the group ran away towards a canal. The incident was witnessed by two persons. An injured eyewitness, another son and the daughter gave detailed accounts describing the role of the accused in beating the family members and the shooting.

value: On the night of 11-12 December 2000, the family had gone to bed after dinner around 9 pm. A quarrel broke out between the accused and his wife around midnight, which escalated into an assault around 1 am. The quarrel reportedly arose from the accused's frustration over the sale of family property and his accusations against his wife. During the assault the accused used a sharp-edged cutting weapon on his wife, who was pregnant, causing numerous incised wounds. The accused's mother intervened to save the wife and was also cut with the weapon. The noise and cries woke the couple's young daughter, who was sleeping in an adjacent room and began to cry. The accused went into that room and struck the child, who sustained two injuries, including a fracture, and died. The wife testified as an injured eyewitness to the sequence of events and stated that she did not see the accused strike the child. A post-mortem found the cause of death to be coma resulting from head injuries sustained 24 to 36 hours earlier, consistent with the blunt side of a weapon. Medical reports recorded fifteen injuries on the wife, who was hospitalised for about one and a half months, and six injuries on the mother, two of whose fingers were later amputated. After the incident the accused bolted the doors from inside, refused to open them to police, and threatened to kill anyone who entered. Police, assisted by villagers, forced the door open and found the accused inside the house armed with an Aruval, with the injured women and the child in the house. An observation mahazar recorded writings on the inner walls of the house. Prosecution witnesses, including the mother, gave evidence about the accused's treatment for mental health concerns.

value: The accused was the commanding officer of a military supply depot whose butchery supplied dressed meat, obtained from a private contractor, to indenting army units. The butchery was run by a supervisory officer, a veterinary officer, junior commissioned and non-commissioned officers, and the accused had overall charge of the depot. After complaints about irregularities, a team of three officers from a central investigating agency and two army officers carried out a surprise inspection of the butchery on 14 February 1990. The inspection team checked eleven vehicles returning from the butchery with meat. Of 1411.2 kg of dressed meat issued to various units, 14.5 kg was found to be heart, which was not an acceptable part of the carcass under the contract's special conditions. During discussions with the inspecting officers, the accused remarked that, to the best of the accused's knowledge, heart was an edible offal that could be issued on demand of units. The accused repeated this in a confidential report dated 15 February 1990. The prosecution case was that this remark amounted to accepting heart as part of the dressed meat with intent to defraud the government. There was no evidence that the accused had instructed heart to be accepted or that heart was regularly accepted. The supervisory and veterinary officers were separately charge-sheeted and punished. The prosecution also alleged that reserve stocks of animals were not maintained in the butchery between 11 and 22 March 1990, and that passed animals were not segregated from the contractor's other animals, contrary to the butchery's standard operating procedure.

value: The accused lived in a rented house with the victim (the accused's brother), the victim's wife and their three children. A neighbour living in an adjoining tenancy in the same building reported a quarrel between the accused and the victim at about 9.00 to 9.15 p.m., during which the accused said he would deal with the victim later. The shopkeeper testified about the sale, but said he did not remember the buyer well and did not know where the buyer lived. A goldsmith said to have sold cyanide to the accused was examined, but he testified that police had coerced him into making his statement. A statement attributed to the accused before police, witnessed by two panch witnesses, was repudiated; one panch witness did not support it. An empty Limca bottle was later recovered from a shelf in the couple's bedroom and was found to contain cyanide, but the bottle reached the laboratory weeks after its recovery.

value: Around mid-afternoon the victim and his brother boarded the same bus, having met by chance, with about ten to fifteen other passengers on board. value: On an afternoon in April 2000, the victim, a sitting state legislator, was riding as a pillion passenger on a motorcycle driven by an informant on a road near a coal-handling site. The informant heard a gunshot from behind and saw a black motorcycle without a registration number running alongside on the left. It was driven by the accused, with a second man on the pillion holding a pistol. The pillion rider fired at close range; the victim was struck in the head, slumped onto the informant, and both men fell to the road. The driver stopped a short distance ahead. The second man walked back, threatened the informant to leave, fired another shot at the victim, pushed the body down the roadside slope, and both men rode away towards a nearby town. Two bystanders who arrived afterwards stated that they had earlier seen the accused riding the same unregistered motorcycle with a pillion passenger in the area. The informant's motorcycle was seized from the scene. A second black unregistered motorcycle was seized from premises linked to the accused; its registration certificate was in another person's name. Two 9 mm empty cartridges were recovered from the scene. The informant's blood-stained T-shirt and torn jeans were seized. A medical examination that evening recorded injuries consistent with a fall. The post-mortem recorded gunshot wounds to the head as the cause of death. The informant identified the pillion rider in court, and one bystander identified him in a test identification parade. Investigators did not send the clothing to a forensic laboratory or the cartridges to a ballistics expert, and the weapon was never recovered. Evidence of a dispute over a petrol pump and of the victim's action against coal theft was also given.

value: On 29 December 1998, at about 5 p.m., the accused allegedly poured kerosene on the body of the victim, who was his wife, and set her on fire. Two persons immediately took the victim to a hospital, where a doctor treated her and informed the police station. A police sub-inspector went to the hospital and recorded a dying declaration. In it the victim stated that the accused often drank liquor, quarrelled with her and assaulted her when drunk. On the same day the accused had given her Rs. 200 for groceries and taken back Rs. 100 of it, so she bought groceries with the remaining Rs. 100. Later that day he returned, demanded the Rs. 100 back and asked her to return the groceries. When she refused, he became angry, tied her hands, poured kerosene on her body and set her ablaze. The victim died of the burn injuries on 19 January 1999. The treating doctor endorsed that the victim was in a fit mental condition to depose before the police. A Forensic Science Laboratory report found kerosene residue on the victim's brassiere, saree and petticoat. The two persons who took the victim to hospital turned hostile during their testimony. No second dying declaration was recorded before a Magistrate. The accused offered no explanation for the kerosene found on the victim's clothing, and no suggestion of suicide or accident was put forward.

The victim and the injured man were taken to a hospital in a truck, and the victim died on the way. A doctor who examined the injured man at the initial stage declared him unfit to make a statement. A doctor conducted the post-mortem and recorded a small red abrasion on the right shoulder region, which was attributed to one of the men said to be carrying a lathi. value: The victim, a married woman, died within the matrimonial home. The prosecution case rested entirely on circumstantial evidence. Several witnesses who were relatives of the victim, including the victim's father, a cousin and a brother, deposed that the victim had been subjected to consistent ill-treatment at the matrimonial home. According to their evidence, the accused was having an illicit relationship with a sister-in-law, and when the victim complained about this, the victim was tortured. The victim had written letters to her father complaining of this ill-treatment; one such letter was placed on record as an exhibit. Witnesses also spoke of beating and visible injury marks on the victim. The post-mortem was conducted by a doctor, who recorded two incised injuries on the body: a deep incised wound on the front of the neck, at the level of the thyroid cartilage, which had completely cut the trachea and cut major neck veins, and a second incised wound on the upper right side of the abdomen through which the small intestine protruded. The doctor's evidence was that these injuries were sufficient to cause death. The body showed some petrification because of the time gap between death and the post-mortem examination. The victim's identity was confirmed by the father, a cousin and a brother, and the hospital released the body to the father, who had it cremated. The defence case was that the victim had been suffering from jaundice and died a natural death. The only witness called in support was not shown to be a medical practitioner and stated only that the victim had been referred for treatment to Patna on 02.09.1993; no record of jaundice treatment was produced.

value: The victim, a woman who had married a man against her family's wishes, lived with her husband and young child in a house owned by another family. About six years after the marriage, the accused, a paternal uncle of the victim, telephoned the victim on 14 August 2002, saying her grandmother was seriously ill and that he would come to pick her up. A household member was sent to a telephone booth to guide him. The accused arrived, was brought to the house, and was introduced by the victim as her uncle. The victim left with the accused on a white scooter, leaving her young son behind. Her husband returned that evening and was told she had gone with the accused. She did not return that night or the next day. The husband lodged a report on 16 August 2002 that she had gone to relatives and had not been seen since. Her body was recovered later that day. A second report then recorded the husband's suspicion, for the first time, that the accused had lured her away and killed her. A post-mortem found death by asphyxia due to smothering, with her scarf pushed into her mouth. The accused was arrested on 7 September 2002, and jewellery the victim was said to have been wearing when she disappeared was recovered from the accused's pockets. The prosecution relied on last-seen testimony from household members and a press reporter who saw the victim and the accused at a bus stand, on the jewellery recovery, and on the post-mortem findings. Witnesses who had seen the accused gave statements to a magistrate about four months later, and one witness identified the accused in court more than two years after the event.

value: The victim had constructed shop rooms on his own land for letting out. A group of men demanded Rs. 40,000 from him as a payment connected with the construction and threatened him with dire consequences if it was not paid. The threats were repeated over several weeks, including at the victim's house, and on 27 September the group said they would murder him if the money was not paid within a day. On the night of 29 September the victim left home on his bicycle to collect money from a business contact and set out for home around 11 p.m. Near a field on his route he was stopped by a group of men and an altercation followed. Eyewitnesses saw several of the accused strangle him with a gumcha. The body was then cut into pieces with a sharp cutting weapon and packed into gunny bags. On the following evening, witnesses saw several of the accused loading the gunny bags into a steel-coloured Maruti van at a rickshaw stand. Two gunny bags containing body parts were later found by a passer-by, who reported them to the police. The victim's wife and brother lodged a missing diary report and later identified the body. The van driver was arrested and the van was recovered on his statement. The victim's bicycle and a chopper were recovered on the statements of accused persons. Post-mortem found death due to ligature strangulation and that all body parts belonged to one person. Several accused absconded for a long period and were arrested later from other places. At identification, eyewitnesses identified all the accused in court, while the van driver did not identify one accused.

value: On the night of 26 May 1980, at about 10.45 p.m., two local residents who were guarding their colony nearby heard screams from a bus stand about 250 yards away and ran to the spot. They said they saw the accused pouring acid on the victim, who was suffering burn injuries. They said the accused was heard saying he would pay a sum of money that day. When the witnesses approached, the accused tried to run away but was caught by bystanders. The accused and the victim were taken to a police station by about 11.10 p.m., and a complaint by one of the witnesses led to an FIR under s.326 IPC. An officer recorded the victim's statement within about ten minutes so that he could be sent to hospital. In that statement the victim said the accused had thrown acid on him. A doctor examined the victim and recorded superficial burns on the face, neck, tongue, back, and other parts of the body. The victim died the next day from the burns, and a post-mortem was conducted. The investigating officer inspected the scene and collected an acid bottle, a bag, and gloves. A chemical report found acid on burnt rubber gloves. No acid marks were found on the accused's body. The defence pointed to the absence of a street light on the site plan, the victim's tongue injury, and the failure to seize the victim's clothes for chemical examination.

value: The victim was admitted to a hospital with serious burn injuries after a fire at the matrimonial home. The investigating police officer obtained a doctor's endorsement that the victim was fit to make a statement. A Sub-Divisional Judicial Magistrate then recorded the victim's statement at the hospital in question-and-answer form, and the victim's thumb impression was taken on it and identified by the investigating officer. In the statement the victim said that the accused, the victim's husband, had often beaten the victim while under the influence of liquor and had demanded money from the victim's father to buy a car. The victim said that on the morning of the incident the accused poured kerosene oil on the victim's body and set it on fire, and that the victim's father-in-law and sister-in-law came and helped put out the fire. The accused's mother was said to have instigated the accused. The victim died a few days later. The post-mortem examination found superficial to deep burns covering about 75 per cent of the body, sparing the lower thighs, legs and feet, and concluded that the burns were ante-mortem and sufficient to cause death. The victim's father, mother and sister were examined at trial but did not fully support the prosecution. The father said the accused had demanded money for a vehicle and that he had refused. The mother said the victim was never harassed for dowry. The sister of the accused said the victim caught fire while preparing tea and that the accused was not at home. The investigating officer, the magistrate and other police witnesses gave evidence on the recording of the statement and the investigation.

value: On 7 December 1998, at about 10.45 p.m., a police sub-inspector returning from duty on his motorcycle reportedly saw three men chasing another man near a bar. The officer, about 30 yards away, said one of the attackers told another to run because police were coming, and the group fled into a nearby conservancy area. An identity card in the victim's pockets identified him. The officer then lodged a written complaint at the police station, on which the first information report was registered. The investigating officer recorded witness statements and recovered knives and blood-soaked earth, and the items were sent to the forensic laboratory. The post-mortem recorded ten stab injuries to the chest, with death attributed to shock and haemorrhage. Several eyewitnesses later did not support the officer's account. The recovery memos lacked the accused's signatures on the disclosure statements, and the recovery witnesses did not support the recoveries. One knife recovered at another accused's instance was blood-stained, but it was not established whether the blood was human or of the victim's blood group. The head constable, the constable and the doctor were not examined, and no forensic expert testified.

value: On an evening in April 2004, the victim rode a motorcycle to the accused's house, where the accused and two daughters were chatting outside. When the accused asked why the victim had come, the victim reportedly said he wished to marry both of the accused's daughters and challenged the accused to say to whom they would be given. Angered, the accused fetched a long knife from the bedroom and struck the victim several times. The victim collapsed and died there. The accused, accompanied by the two daughters, travelled to a police station on a two-wheeler and handed over the knife to the station writer, stating that the victim had been killed with it. A first information statement was registered on that basis. The victim's body, with multiple bleeding wounds, was found in the compound of the accused's house. The knife was seized in the presence of a steel plant technician. A forensic laboratory found human blood on the knife, though its blood group could not be traced. The post-mortem doctor recorded seventeen injuries, thirteen of them incised cut wounds, and opined death from shock and haemorrhage; the doctor said the wounds could have been caused by a knife like the one recovered. The two daughters had been examined as eyewitnesses but did not support the first information statement when examined in court. The accused had been living apart from the spouse, who lived with her parents together with the daughters, and the victim had been staying in the same house as them. The accused had strained relations with the victim's mother. The accused asserted an alibi of shopping with the daughters, which was not corroborated.

value: The victim, a railway official, lived in an official bungalow with his wife, son and daughter. A domestic servant employed by him lived in the servant quarters and allegedly held a grudge against the victim's wife. He allegedly planned with relatives and an associate to kill the family and take cash and jewellery. According to the prosecution, on the day in question the servant admitted several people to the house while the victim was at work. Armed with knives and a pistol, the group killed the son, the wife and the daughter in turn, and one of the group was shot during a struggle. When the victim returned from work in the evening, he was also killed. The bedroom almirah was broken open and cash and jewellery were taken. The bodies and blood-stained clothing were placed in a car, which was driven to a railway track area, doused with petrol bought from a petrol pump, and set on fire. Visitors were turned away with conflicting explanations. Investigators found the walls and floor blood-stained and the floor washed with phenyl and acid. Chance fingerprints matching the accused were lifted from the bedroom almirah. Items including a pistol, cartridges, knives, a cell phone and gold ornaments were recovered after statements by the accused. A forensic expert found human blood and flammable traces. A ballistics expert linked the cartridges to the recovered pistol. A doctor treated an injured accused, who attributed the gunshot injury to a fall. No eyewitness saw the killings.

value: A girl aged about five to six years was found dead on a cot in a village where she was staying with her blind, infirm maternal grandmother, who was too poor and unable to care for her. The girl's grandmother's thatched house had collapsed, so the grandmother and the girl used to sleep in a house very close by, which belonged to the accused. The victim's mother was first told the girl had died of paralysis, and the body was buried on a riverbank. Later, the mother received information from several villagers that the girl had been raped and killed by the accused, and she asked for the body to be exhumed. After an order of the Sub-Divisional Magistrate, the body was dug out and examined on 3.2.1996 by two doctors. They found multiple contusions on the face, neck, shoulder and back, and vaginal injuries including lacerations, and stated that the death was caused by shock and haemorrhage from ante-mortem vaginal injuries. One witness deposed that he had been returning home at about 9.00 p.m. with a companion, heard whispering near the accused's house, and focused a torch and saw the accused raping the girl beneath a tree outside the house. The companion raised a cry, villagers gathered, and the accused ran away. Another witness deposed that the accused had confessed the crime to him in the presence of two others. A part of a bed sheet and white cloth were recovered during the investigation, and forensic examination found human blood and semen on them, as well as on a vaginal swab taken by the doctor. The accused was arrested at a road junction in the early hours of the following day while waiting for transport. Several other witnesses did not support the prosecution account.

value: The victim was married in June 2002 in an arranged marriage. At the marriage, a dowry of Rs 25,000 was promised by the victim's side; Rs 15,000 was paid then and the balance of Rs 10,000 was promised within about four months. The victim's father could not pay the balance. The prosecution alleged that the accused, the victim's spouse and mother-in-law, pressed for the balance, harassed the victim for non-payment, refused to send the victim to the parental home, and that the victim had told relatives about the ill-treatment. A witness said that the couple was happy for the first months and that quarrels followed. On one visit to the parental home, the spouse demanded a fan, a ring and Rs 1,000 in cash, along with the balance dowry; when these were not met, the spouse left the victim there. On 15 February 2003, around 11 a.m., the accused left a witness in the house on an errand. When the witness returned, the victim was found hanging from a beam with a saree. The victim's parents came, cut the victim down and took the victim to hospital, where the victim was declared dead. Police registered the report, seized the saree used for hanging, photographed the scene and arranged a post-mortem. The doctor found an oblique ligature mark on the front and left sides of the neck and an abrasion on the chin, all antemortem, and recorded asphyxia from hanging as the cause of death. The victim's father's account was corroborated by two other witnesses. One witness stated that the dowry of Rs 15,000 was handed over at the marriage and that the balance was not paid. The witnesses described the persistent dowry demands and beating and abuse of the victim.

value: In the early hours of 14 June 2004, at about 2 to 2.30 a.m., a group of men entered the house of the victims. The victim's brother-in-law was beaten with knives, an iron rod and a wooden club and died from his injuries. When the victim, the brother-in-law's sister-in-law, began shouting, the assailants turned on her and struck her on the eyes, head and back. She was left seriously injured and could not speak when brought to hospital. She told police that four to five men were involved, wearing pants and shirts, and that they fled on a motorcycle. At trial, in cross-examination, she stated that the number of persons was five. She identified the accused in court and described the clothing and physical features of the attackers. Police had earlier stopped a motorcycle carrying three fleeing men; two were apprehended, one of them the accused, and a third escaped. At the time of arrest, a knife, a motorcycle key and cash were seized from the accused, and the seizure was witnessed by a panch witness. The accused's clothes were examined and found to have blood stains. The victim's husband stated that cash of about Rs.4,000 to 5,000 and the ornaments worn by the victim were taken, and a spot panchnama recorded in his presence noted disturbed household articles and a forced window. A post-mortem doctor gave evidence on the head injuries and cause of death and on the injuries to the victim. The motorcycle used by the group had been stolen earlier and was recovered. Two of the men were juveniles and were dealt with separately, and two others remained absconding. Charge sheet was filed against the accused and the others.

value: The victim, a married woman, died from extensive burn injuries within 35 days of her marriage to the accused. Hospital records noted that, according to the accused, she was burned by a stove while preparing tea and bread in the kitchen. A post-mortem examination recorded first-degree burns extending from the top of the head to the tip of the leg, and the examining doctor gave evidence. Police recovered from the kitchen a 20-litre cane with about a litre of kerosene, a quilt, pillows, a piece of cloth soaked in kerosene, and the victim's clothes, which smelled of kerosene. The prosecution alleged that shortly after the marriage the accused demanded Rs.40,000 from the victim's father for business purposes. The father refused, and the accused remarked that he knew how to obtain money through his own daughter. The accused later pledged the victim's jewels with a third party for Rs.11,000. The victim was also alleged to be upset about the accused's illicit relationship with his niece, who lived in the same house. Several witnesses, including the victim's father, a neighbour, a cousin and a relative, testified that the victim had complained to them about the money demands, the relationship and her unhappiness in the marriage. The prosecution case was that the victim poured kerosene on herself and set herself on fire because of this pressure from the accused.

value: An application for a water connection in the name of a constable's wife was cleared at a lower level and the file was then sent to the accused, a junior engineer in a water board. The complainant, a police constable who was the applicant's husband, lodged a report with the anti-corruption branch alleging that the accused had demanded a bribe of Rs. 2000 to clear the file, with Rs. 1000 to be paid initially and the balance after clearance. A trap was laid. According to the prosecution, the accused demanded and accepted Rs. 1000 as the bribe. This led to registration of a first information report under Sections 7 and 13 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. After investigation, a charge-sheet was submitted in September 2002. In parallel, a departmental inquiry was initiated on the same allegation that the accused had demanded, accepted and obtained Rs. 1000 as illegal gratification in consideration of giving a report on the water connection. The inquiry officer recorded that the evidence on record did not substantiate the charge of demand and acceptance of bribe, and found the charge not proved due to lack of evidence on record.

value: A State Special Rehabilitation Package provided cash benefit in two instalments to persons displaced by a submerged dam project, to help them buy land. The second instalment was payable only after both seller and purchaser registered a sale deed and submitted proof of registration. Complaints alleged that various fake sale deeds were registered at the Registrar's office in Khargone to claim the benefit, and that beneficiaries were not affected by the project. A Collector's inquiry reported that some vendors were fictitious persons and that deeds were executed and registered fraudulently. Several FIRs were registered on a rehabilitation officer's complaint. The FIR for one registration recorded that a beneficiary received Rs.3,39,857 after a registration whose survey number was wrong and whose vendor could not be traced in the village. A departmental enquiry was then conducted, and it recorded procedural irregularities in registration, such as accepting photocopies of documents and not obtaining PAN details. The investigating officer alleged that the accused, a registering officer, had abetted the conspiracy and misused his position. The investigation was still continuing, and the charge-sheet stated that the accused's handwriting report and the district registrar's statement were awaited.

value: On a morning at about 7 a.m., the victim went to a nearby house to discuss the proposed marriage of his granddaughter to a son of the woman of that house. After the discussion, as the victim came out, a group of persons who had been sitting in another nearby house came out, approached him, scolded him about the marriage arrangement, and assaulted him with an axe, stones and sticks. Several relatives and villagers who came to rescue the victim were also assaulted and sustained injuries. The attack ended after police intervention. The victim was taken by bullock cart to a hospital and then referred to a civil hospital, where he died the same evening, about twelve hours after the assault. He remained unconscious throughout that time and no dying declaration was recorded. A complaint was lodged with the police later that night. The doctor who conducted the post-mortem stated that the probable cause of death was primarily head injury associated with other multiple injuries, and that some stick injuries and an axe injury were identified. Doctors examined the injuries of some accused and found them minor. Eyewitness testimony came from the victim's brother, who was also injured, the victim's son, who witnessed the occurrence, and the mother-in-law of the granddaughter's fiancé, each describing the overt acts of particular accused.

value: On a day in October 1997, the accused and a companion went to a family's residence intending to commit robbery. While the companion stood guard outside, the accused entered and found the eleven-year-old daughter of the household. He caught hold of her neck, threatened to kill her, and robbed her of a gold chain and two gold ear studs. He then entered a bedroom where the victim, an elderly woman aged about 90, lay on a cot and tried to take her ornaments. When the victim raised an alarm, the accused pulled her down from the cot and struck her on the head with a wall clock. He broke a gold chain from her neck and took two imitation bangles from a bag in an almirah, then left. The girl told her father, and they returned with friends. The victim was taken to a government hospital and then a medical college hospital, where she died nine days after the incident. The treating civil surgeon recorded a forehead injury with suspicion of fracture and eyelid swelling, consistent with a wall clock blow. A forensic doctor attributed death to the head injuries. The girl gave consistent eyewitness testimony corroborating her father. Two neighbours, both declared hostile, admitted seeing the accused near the house that day. The investigating officer recovered the stolen gold ornaments at the accused's instance. No test identification parade was held. The girl identified the accused in court.

value: The victim was married to the accused and died of burn injuries within seven years of the marriage. The victim's father filed a written complaint the day after the death, alleging that the accused and the accused's family had harassed the victim over dowry demands from the early days of the marriage. He also alleged that the in-laws had earlier tried to set the victim on fire and that neighbours had rescued her. The victim was admitted to hospital with burns all over the body and died during treatment the same afternoon. The postmortem examination recorded extensive burns as the cause of death. A witness stated that the accused used to beat the victim for dowry. The victim's father stated that the accused had beaten and harassed the victim for dowry after the marriage, and had earlier confined the victim in a room and tried to burn her alive by pouring kerosene; family members apologised and assured that it would not recur. The victim's mother testified that the couple visited her village about a month before the death and that the victim asked her to send her father because the accused harassed her. Other witnesses stated that the marriage took place about six or seven years earlier. A case was registered, investigated, and a charge sheet was filed.

value: The accused and the victim's family lived in the same village and owned adjoining agricultural land. A dispute existed over the use of a way to reach their fields. On the morning of the incident, the victim and the complainant attempted to reach their field to sow seeds but were obstructed by one of the accused, who abused and threatened them. Later that day, the complainant was told by a neighbour that several of the accused were waiting on a road to assault the victim. The complainant rode a bicycle to the spot and, from about 200 metres away, saw a group beating the victim with a cycle chain and stones while abusing him. The group then turned on the complainant and assaulted him with a cycle chain and stones until a bystander intervened. The complainant found the victim bleeding heavily from the head and with beating marks over the body. The victim was taken to a rural hospital, where he was declared dead. The post-mortem recorded 19 external and 4 internal injuries, all ante-mortem, with death due to shock from haemorrhage. The doctor stated that some injuries were caused by a cycle chain and others by stones, and that the injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course to cause death. The complainant's 11 injuries were certified by the same doctor and attributed to hard blunt objects and a cycle chain. Police arrested the accused, seized blood-stained clothing, and recovered the cycle chain and stones on the basis of information from the accused. Chemical analysis detected human blood on the clothing of the accused and the victim, although the blood group of the accused's sample was inconclusive. A second eyewitness supported the complainant's account. In oral evidence the complainant named fewer assailants than in his written complaint.

value: The prosecution case is that the victim disliked a man visiting his house and suspected him of having an illicit relationship with the victim's wife. The victim had forbidden the man from coming to the house and threatened to kill him if he returned. About two days before the incident the man came again and the victim repeated the threat. On the day of the incident, around noon, the victim was sitting in front of a roadside eatery near a bus stand. Two witnesses had just finished taking tea there and saw a verbal altercation between the victim and two accused, one of whom was the man's father. During the altercation, one accused threw a stone which struck the victim on the head. The victim fell, and the other accused struck him several times with a sword, injuring his neck, head and face. People nearby ran away. Witnesses said the attackers fled believing the victim dead. Witnesses tried to help the victim, who was bleeding heavily, and took him to a police station and then toward a hospital, where he died en route. Police witnesses prepared a site plan and seized items from the spot, including the sword and the stone. The post-mortem found several ante-mortem external injuries, including a frontal bone fracture, a crush injury to the cheek, and a neck wound with a vertebral fracture. The doctor opined the injuries were sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course. The doctor stated that the crush injury could be caused by the stone and the other injuries by the sword. A forensic report found human blood on the blade of the sword and on the stone.

value: The victim was married to the accused in February 1990. The accused was serving in the army and stayed at the matrimonial home only while on leave. The prosecution case was that, soon after the marriage, the accused demanded a motorcycle as dowry and threatened that the victim would not be allowed to remain in the matrimonial home if the demand was not met. Relatives of the victim, including her brother and a village companion, intervened and pacified the accused on more than one occasion. In the days before the victim's death in September 1993, the demand was renewed, the accused harassed the victim and beat her. On 16 September 1993 the accused's brother visited the victim's brother's village and reported that the victim had died after suffering an electric shock. When the victim's brother and others reached the matrimonial village, they learned that the body had already been cremated. Enquiries led the victim's brother to conclude that the victim had been killed for dowry by the accused and the accused's mother. A first information report was lodged on 19 September 1993 and the accused was arrested the same day. The evidence consisted of oral testimony from the victim's brother, a village companion, the victim's father and another witness about the dowry demand and the cruelty, and evidence from the village Sarpanch about the cremation. No doctor who allegedly attended the victim was examined and no medical evidence on the cause of death was produced. The electrocution explanation rested on the accused's brother, who did not testify, and the accused did not mention electrocution in his statement under section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

value: The victim, aged 21, had known the accused for about four months. On 15.2.2007 the accused telephoned her at about 8.45 pm and asked her to meet him at Lodhi Colony, New Delhi. She felt inebriated and alleged that the accused touched her breasts and continued to misbehave despite her objections. A medical examination on 21.2.2007 recorded that she had no external injuries and her hymen was not intact. No vaginal smear was taken because more than a month had elapsed, and her clothes were not sent for forensic examination because she had changed them. The police could not recover the drink container, glass or undergarments, and no blood sample was sent for analysis. Mobile phone call records showed that the accused was at Noida and Ghaziabad, including a function from 9.15 pm to 11.30 pm on 15.2.2007, and that no calls were made by him to the victim that day. Her call records placed her at other locations in Delhi and in conversation with friends. A tenancy verification affidavit described her as married. The victim's statement was recorded under section 164 CrPC on 27.2.2007.

Police stopped the bus, and the accused first gave a false name before giving his true name. value: The victim, a seven-year-old boy, left home for school one morning in mid-April and did not return. His father searched relatives and the school without success and reported the boy missing to the police the same day. About five days later, the body of a boy was found on a hillock. The body had been partly eaten by animals, the right hand and head were missing, and the father identified the body from the clothes, shoes, socks and school bag. Three witnesses, two goldsmiths and a firewood collector, said they saw the victim in the company of three men, including the accused, on a scooter or walking towards the hillock around midday. The witnesses knew the accused and the victim, and one witness was cross-examined at length without any contradiction of his account. Following information given by one of the accused, a blood-stained pant and shirt were recovered from that accused's house in the presence of two witnesses. A forensic report found the blood on them to be of human origin. The victim's family had a prior dispute with the accused over a neighbourhood incident in which a girl died after consuming poison. One accused had threatened to finish the victim's family. The victim's mother said she saw the accused with a scooter near her house on the day the victim went missing.

value: The prosecution alleged that two accused, acting with a third person who later became an accomplice prosecution witness, planned to kill the owner of a hair salon whom they blamed for interfering in one accused's marital troubles. One accused had threatened to kill the owner within a week, and the other joined in that threat. The third person allegedly left a cardboard box containing a tape recorder loaded with explosive at the salon, saying he would return for it. Shortly afterwards, an employee switched on the device, which exploded with a loud sound, damaging the premises. The employee died from his injuries, and two other employees were injured. The prosecution relied on the accomplice's account; the testimony of a relative who said he saw the accused collect the box, pay for it and later hear them admit planting a bomb; the statements of the injured; and a doctor who described the injuries as caused by the blast. Forensic analysis of recovered debris and clothing reportedly detected nitroglycerine, nitrocellulose and ammonium nitrate. Investigators also found that gelatin sticks and detonators had been bought and that a tape recorder had been purchased from a shop.

value: On an evening in late April, four men stopped the victim and a second man while they were walking home at a park centre. The previous day, the same parties had quarrelled while the victim and the second man were collecting palmyrah nuts from fields. A shopkeeper in the vicinity intervened and pacified them, though one of the accused allegedly threatened the victim with dire consequences. On the following evening, the accused allegedly confronted the victim and the second man. Three of the accused were armed with stout casuarina sticks; the fourth was unarmed. An altercation followed, and one accused allegedly struck the victim on the head. When the second man intervened, two others allegedly struck him on the head with sticks. Both men fell. The fourth accused allegedly kicked and punched the victim, while the three armed men continued hitting both of them. The assailants then ran away towards the house of one of them, believing both men dead. Four persons were said to have witnessed the incident. The injured were taken to a government hospital, where the victim's statement was recorded. The victim died of his injuries in the early hours of the next day. The investigation included arrest of the accused, post-mortem examination of the body, and seizure of the weapons of offence.

value: On 18 February 2005 at about 6:30 p.m. the victim went to fields near her village to ease herself and did not return. Her family searched but could not find her. During the search the accused was found in the fields. When the victim's mother asked him where her daughter was, he did not respond and ran away from the place. He could not be traced in the village until 21 February 2005, when he was reportedly produced and arrested. The victim's body was found the next morning in daylight in fields belonging to another person, with her neck wrapped in a blue shawl that belonged to her. The family had earlier had a dispute with the accused: some years before, he and a cousin had teased the victim's elder sister on a path, the matter was taken to a village panchayat, and both apologised; the accused was said to have later threatened revenge. Medical examination showed death by asphyxia due to strangulation, ante-mortem and sufficient to cause death. There were multiple abrasions and contusions on the face, chin and back. Forensic examination found blood on the shawl, salwar and underwear of the victim. Human semen was detected on a vaginal swab from the victim. The accused's underwear, taken on his examination after arrest, also showed human semen. The medical evidence indicated the victim had been subjected to sexual intercourse before her death.

value: The victim had developed an illicit relationship with the accused's wife. After the accused learned of it, relatives held a meeting, the matter was apparently settled, and the victim was told to leave the area. A witness said the accused had threatened that if the accused could lay hands on the victim, the accused would chop the victim into pieces. On 15 February 2005 the victim was seen in the company of a co-accused, first at a bar and then at a roadside food stall. Witnesses at the food stall said the accused arrived in a Maruti van with other men, drank coffee, and then followed the motorcycle carrying the victim and the co-accused. An auto-rickshaw driver saw a van parked on a road that night with a man standing beside it, and another driver saw two men take a pillion rider into a van. The victim was not seen again. Between 16 and 19 February 2005, parts of a body, including legs, a torso, hands and a head, were found floating in a lake. The victim's father and others identified the remains, and DNA testing of the parents' samples matched the limbs. A chopper was recovered from the lake on the accused's disclosure, and the accused personally retrieved it. A skull was found after digging at a place the accused showed investigators. A glove and plastic rope were also recovered at the accused's instance. A Maruti van was recovered, and hair found in it matched the victim. A forensic surgeon opined that the chopper could have caused the dismemberment. The serologist could not determine the blood group on the chopper. A witness testified that the accused had borrowed the van and returned it later, and call records between the accused and that witness were proved. A letter purportedly written by the victim was posted at a post office, and a witness saw the accused post it.

value: The victim was married to the accused in February 1996. The victim's father alleged that after the marriage the victim was subjected to physical and mental torture by the accused and the accused's family for not getting sufficient dowry. Gold jewellery, silver items, furniture and other gifts were said to have been given at the marriage. On 2 April 1999 the victim's father went to the accused's house with relatives, and he alleged he was abused and physically pushed out. On 4 April 1999 the victim's father was told by telephone that the victim had suffered severe burn injuries and died at the accused's house. An FIR was lodged the same day and the police registered a case and investigated. At trial, the victim's father, the victim's cousin and the victim's mother testified. The father and mother stated that about six months after the marriage the victim reported that the accused had demanded Rs.50,000 to buy a computer for a business. The prosecution witnesses made general allegations of harassment but identified no specific acts of cruelty. The accused gave evidence that, while cleaning the house, he found a handwritten chit bearing the victim's handwriting and signature. The chit stated that nobody was responsible for the victim's death, that the victim's parents and family had harassed the accused, and that the victim was tired of life because of quarrels.

value: The accused and the victim had married, and the marriage was not approved by the victim's family and was strained. The couple had started divorce proceedings by mutual consent, with the second hearing listed for the following day. On the day before that hearing, the accused visited the hostel where the victim lived and worked. The two spoke for about an hour in the verandah, after which the accused left alone. Later, the victim was found dead among plants in the hostel grounds. The victim's father, who came to the hostel, was told by hostel staff that the accused had visited. A complaint was lodged, and police recovered the body and nearby objects, including a rope. The post-mortem examination found death by asphyxia caused by smothering and throttling, with neck abrasions and fractures of the neck and chest. Calls were later made from the victim's mobile phone to her mother and other relatives, in which the caller said he had killed her and would commit suicide. The accused was traced to a guest house, where he had registered under a fictitious name and address. He tried to end his life there and ran away, leaving a diary, a letter and a wrist watch, which contained writings about his grievances with the victim's family. The victim's mobile phone was later recovered from a shop in another state, following the accused's disclosure, and call records showed it was used after the death. Hair found at the scene was reported as similar to the accused's sample. The accused declined a test identification parade.

value: The victim went out to graze cows and did not return by dusk; the next morning his body was found with injuries in a jungle. The police registered a case, held an inquest, and during investigation a labourer who worked under the victim was apprehended and made a statement implicating two men. The principal evidence is the account of an eyewitness who was grazing cows with the victim in a rubber garden around 2 p.m. At about 4 p.m. the two accused arrived armed with an axe, a lathi and a gun. The first accused struck the victim with the axe; the second struck him with a stick; and the first then took a gun from the jungle and shot him. The eyewitness fled, stating he was afraid because the accused had threatened him with dire consequences if he disclosed the incident. He later told another villager, and subsequently gave a statement to police. A witness stated that around 1.30 p.m. he had seen the victim and the accused grazing cows nearby. The investigating officer's inquest report recorded injuries caused by an axe and a gun. He also recovered the handle of an axe near the body and seized it under a seizure list prepared in the presence of witnesses. Blood-stained wooden sticks and a takkal dao were also found near the body. A charge-sheet was filed against the two accused.

value: The victim had been married to one accused for about eight years and had four children. The victim's family had given dowry at the wedding, but the victim was allegedly harassed for more, including after a sister's wedding about fifteen days before the incident. On the night of 14 May 1998, around 11 p.m., a quarrel took place at the accused's house. It is alleged that one accused placed a leg on the victim's neck and beat the victim, after which the other accused held the victim's hands while the husband sprinkled kerosene and set the victim on fire with a match. A relative was present in the house. The victim was taken to hospital in the early hours of 15 May 1998. On 16 May 1998 a judicial magistrate, after a duty doctor certified the victim fit and conscious, recorded the victim's statement in question-and-answer form, with a toe impression, naming the husband and mother-in-law and describing the dowry harassment. The examining doctor recorded burns over approximately 85% of the body. The victim died of burn injuries on 4 June 1998 at another hospital, and the post-mortem attributed death to burns. Police arrested the husband on 21 May 1998, when he showed doctors burn injuries to his hands; a stove containing kerosene was recovered on his disclosure. The victim's father testified about the in-laws' harassment. A defence witness, a child of the accused, said the fire came from a kerosene stove but admitted the husband was present in the house at the time.

value: According to the prosecution, on the afternoon of 29 March 2000 the victim, a 22-year-old woman, went to a field near an embankment to attend her goats. When she did not return home, her father searched for her along the embankment. While returning, he heard loud laughter from a farm house belonging to the accused. Later he went back to the embankment, shouted for her, and the accused came out of the farm house and looked at him. The father then went down a path and found the victim lying dead on the left side, with a cut injury on her chin and blood oozing from her body. He raised an alarm, and her brother and other villagers gathered. The accused also came to the spot and enquired. The body was taken home, and a Sub-Inspector of Police seized the victim's clothing and prepared a seizure list. The inquest was held and the body was sent for post-mortem. The brother lodged a written complaint at the police out-post, and a case was registered. During investigation, the victim's underwear stained with semen was seized the same day. The accused and an eyewitness labourer were apprehended and interrogated. On the next day, police seized a blue underwear of the accused suspected to have semen stains, a bed sheet, a sporting item and a dao from the farm house. Both underwear items were sent for forensic examination. The post-mortem doctor found death by asphyxia due to throttling, a fractured trachea, bruises on the neck and a cut injury on the chin, and found no spermatozoa in the vaginal smear and no sign of injury on the genital organs. The eyewitness stated that he saw the accused and a companion follow the victim, saw them commit rape and then throttle her, and saw them drag the body into bushes. He said he stayed silent out of fear because both men carried khukris. The victim's father, two brothers and co-villagers gave corroborative evidence about the body and the scene.

value: On the evening of 28 June 2001, a group of about 25 to 30 persons from the village gathered outside the house where the victims were staying. They were armed with swords, gandasis, sabals and sticks. The group surrounded the house, climbed onto its roof and pelted stones, damaging the roof sheets and tiles. Several of the occupants escaped over a common wall into another room. Around midnight, the informant, his wife, his mother and another woman were made to sit on a neighbouring thatched roof. Shortly afterwards, a further group arrived in a jeep, broke open the door of the informant's house and inflicted blows with swords, gandasis and sticks. Three persons died inside the house. Two others were dragged outside and assaulted on the head, face, hands and feet with gandasis and swords, and both died. The attackers burnt two motorcycles belonging to the victims before leaving. The FIR was lodged at 6.45 a.m. on 29 June 2001. The informant explained that the family was too traumatised during the night to go to the police station. Investigators prepared a site plan, conducted autopsies, seized blood-stained clothing and recorded witness statements. Weapons were recovered on information given by accused persons in custody. The eyewitnesses were the informant and close relatives of the deceased. The defence contended that no independent witness was examined. The motive alleged was suspicion that the victims had killed the son of the village leader, which led to revenge.

value: The victim, a young woman, was a neighbour of the accused in the same village. The victim had lost her mother in early childhood and lived with her brother's family, and her father also lived in the house. The accused used to tease the victim and repeatedly asked her to marry him. On one occasion the victim was alone at home while other family members were at a temple. The accused entered the house and asked for sexual intercourse. The victim refused and said intercourse could only take place after marriage. The accused gagged the victim's mouth with the accused's right hand and had sexual intercourse with the victim. Afterwards the accused told the victim not to reveal the incident to anyone, promising marriage while placing a hand on the victim's head. Over about six months the two were intimate repeatedly at different places, and the accused repeatedly said marriage would follow. During a visit to a temple, the accused refused to marry the victim. The victim told the victim's brother and father, who sought the help of village elders. The elders convened a panchayat and summoned the accused, who again refused to marry. The victim then lodged a complaint with the police on 10 October 2003. Prosecution evidence included the testimony of the victim, the victim's brother and father, four village elders who attended the panchayat, two friends of the accused who had met the victim and the accused at the temple, and a doctor who medically examined the victim.

value: The victim, a female child of about six years, was the daughter of a man who did masonry work. The accused was related to the victim's family and had worked for the victim's father on occasions. A dispute existed between them over wages the accused had received for work he did not perform. On the day of the incident, a witness saw the accused with the victim at the family home at around 10.30 am, with the child seated on his lap. A shopkeeper later saw the accused buy sweets for the child at about 1.15 pm. When the child could not be found that evening, the family searched the accused's house and a nearby village without success. Another child reported seeing the accused taking the victim away, but that child did not testify. Later the accused was brought back to the village by the victim's father. On the way he reportedly said that if he was not beaten he would tell the truth, and stated that he had killed the child over the wage dispute and hidden her body under stones on a mountain. At his instruction, police and witnesses went to the spot in a jeep, where the body was recovered from under stones and branches. It showed bleeding head and ear injuries, and the child was wearing a school uniform. At the accused's instruction a blood-stained shirt was recovered from under a stone on a road, and it bore blood of the same group as the victim. The accused was physically examined and had no injuries. A post-mortem found head injuries that the doctor considered antemortem and homicidal, with the cause of death being shock from cardio-respiratory arrest due to head injuries.

value: In the early hours of the morning on 8 July 2008, while members of a household were asleep in two rooms of a family dwelling, the accused allegedly attacked family members with the separated parts of a pair of sharp scissors. The accused's spouse and two sons were stabbed multiple times and died at the scene. The accused also stabbed the victim, the accused's daughter, multiple times. When the victim asked why she was being hurt, she was told that the whole family had to go and the accused would follow. The accused then gave her water, held her on his lap, and pressed a pillow over her mouth, but she did not die. The accused left her in that condition, bolted the outer door from outside, and went to a police station to report the incident. A neighbouring relative heard the victim calling for help, opened the door and found the deceased lying in pools of blood. The victim was taken to hospital and treated. The post-mortem examination recorded death from haemorrhagic shock with haemothorax due to multiple stab injuries, and the doctor opined that the injuries could have been caused by the scissors. Blood on the accused's clothing matched the blood group of the accused's deceased spouse. The scissors and clothing were recovered on the accused's disclosure, and blood-soaked material was collected from the spot. The accused's statement to the police, recorded at the station, described the killings and gave a reason for them. The investigation included an inquest, a spot panchnama and photographs.

value: The victim, a woman, was married to the accused in April 1989 and lived in the accused's house, where she also worked for a private company. About three months before her death, the accused and the victim reportedly quarrelled because she had not become pregnant after marriage. The prosecution alleged that before the marriage the accused demanded cash of Rs 15,000 and gold and silver ornaments. Part of the cash was handed over before the wedding and more at the wedding, and all ornaments except one pair of gold bangles were given. The balance was promised after marriage. The prosecution alleged that the accused drank liquor and subjected the victim to mental and physical cruelty over the demand for the balance dowry. In March 1990, about eleven months after the marriage, the victim set herself on fire with kerosene in the house early in the morning. The accused informed the police of the unnatural death. An inquest was held by an executive magistrate, who recorded statements from the victim's blood relatives, and a case was registered. The post-mortem found 97% ante-mortem burns and death due to shock, with no signs of pregnancy. The accused was arrested, and during interrogation he led police to a pawnbroker's shop where the victim's pledged ornaments were recovered. Eleven prosecution witnesses were examined, including the victim's sister, brother and brother-in-law, who deposed about the dowry demand and cruelty.
