value: The accused married the victim in 1988 and they lived in a matrimonial house together with the accused's parents and brother. It is alleged that the accused and other household members ill-treated and tortured the victim. During the marriage the victim had a premature delivery. After a later pregnancy in 1993, it is alleged that the accused gave the victim tablets that caused a miscarriage. A child born to the couple did not survive long. On 23 February 1996 the victim poured kerosene over herself and drank some, which was later cleared away. A mediation meeting had been scheduled for that day, and the victim's relatives and a neighbour were to attend. The victim then died by hanging before the meeting took place. A neighbour gave the first information to the police. The case was first registered as an unnatural death and later altered to offences of cruelty and abetment of suicide. The investigating officer seized documents and material objects, examined witnesses, and laid a charge sheet. A post-mortem examination was conducted. The evidence included oral testimony from fifteen witnesses, documentary exhibits, material objects, and evidence that the accused worked abroad and visited India on leave only four times between 1988 and 1996, the last visit being in January-February 1996. The accused had also made efforts toward mediation to settle the differences.

value: The victim was married to the accused in July 2000. After the marriage the victim was allegedly harassed for insufficient dowry, and the accused raised a demand for a motorcycle, in addition to demands made by the accused's mother and younger brother. About three months after the marriage the victim telephoned her father about the demands. The victim's father and uncle met the accused and his relatives and asked that the victim not be harassed, but the harassment continued. In April 2001 the victim again complained by telephone. The uncle brought the victim to her parental home, but the next day the accused came, insisted that the victim be sent back, and threatened divorce; the victim was sent with the accused. On 1 May 2001 the victim's family received word that the victim had suffered burn injuries and had been taken to hospital. There, the victim told the victim's father, uncle and brother-in-law that the victim had been beaten and set on fire by the accused and the accused's family members. The victim died of extensive burn injuries. The victim's father lodged the first information report, and an investigating officer conducted the investigation and sent the accused for trial. The prosecution relied on testimony of relatives about dowry demands, medical evidence and investigation evidence. A suicide note stated that nobody should be held responsible and that all doors were closed for the victim. The defence contended that the victim had taken her own life because of pressure from an uncle over parental property, and that relations with the accused were cordial.

value: On the day of the incident, the victim, aged about fifteen, was alone at home. The victim's mother was away at another village and other family members were not present. One accused came to the house and asked the victim to fetch lassi from the house of another accused and that accused's spouse. When the victim entered that house, two other men already there bolted the door from inside and raped the victim. The victim was held for about an hour and threatened with elimination if the incident was disclosed. The victim did not disclose the incident for about twenty days, until the mother returned from a maternal visit. The victim then told the mother, and the father took the victim to lodge a report at the police station. The report was registered the next day. The investigating officer inspected the spot and recorded the victim's statement before a magistrate under section 164. A medical examination found no external injuries, no injury to the perineum or thighs, and a healed ruptured hymen that admitted one finger easily. A radiological examination assessed the age as between 14 and 16 years. A school certificate recorded a date of birth showing the victim was fifteen at the time. The victim's testimony and the mother's corroborating account of the delayed disclosure were presented.

value: On the early morning of the occurrence, two visitors who had arranged by telephone the previous evening to be taken to a plot for earthwork came to the victim's house. They were let in, and tea was prepared for them at the victim's direction. The visitors asked the victim to accompany them on his scooter. As he started the scooter, both visitors drew pistols from the folds of their garments and fired at him. He fell onto the scooter. The victim's mother and wife were in the house and witnessed the shooting. The assailants ran away, and the mother heard a vehicle starting on the other side of the road. The mother gave a statement to police, which led to registration of the first information report. The investigating officer called a fingerprint expert to the house. The expert found two glass tumblers on the table, smeared with tea. He lifted fingerprints from them, sealed them in a packet, and sent them to the fingerprint bureau. There, the seal was found intact, and the prints were compared with specimen prints of two suspects taken in the presence of a Judicial Magistrate. The comparison found the questioned prints similar to the specimen prints. The autopsy showed a lacerated wound on the left side of the chest. It had blackening around it and perforated the left lung, the upper part of the heart and the right lung. The doctor opined that death resulted from shock and haemorrhage due to a firearm injury. Police recovered two pistols with live cartridges, two empty twelve-bore cartridges, the scooter and a footwear from the spot.

value: The victim, a 28-year-old married woman, was admitted to hospital with extensive burn injuries on the night of 9 December 2003, after kerosene oil was poured on her at her matrimonial home and set alight. Burns covered roughly half her body. Once a doctor certified her fit to give a statement, a Magistrate recorded her statement. She said that at about 9.30 to 10.00 p.m. the accused, a husband, a brother-in-law and the brother-in-law's wife, had poured kerosene oil on her and set her ablaze, and that nobody tried to extinguish the fire. She said the husband had an illicit relationship with the brother-in-law's wife, that she quarrelled with him over it, and that after drinking liquor he beat her with a stick and shoes. Investigators inspected the scene, seized burnt clothing, ash and a kerosene lamp, and obtained post-mortem and forensic reports. The post-mortem doctor attributed death to ante-mortem burns sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature. A medical examiner noted superficial deep burns across the body and said burns from kerosene falling on the head could not be ruled out. The victim's father testified to dowry harassment, earlier divorce proceedings, panchayat settlements and a telephone call a week before the incident seeking to return to her parents' home. The victim's brother supported this account. No eyewitness saw the incident. The defence case was that the burns were accidental, caused by a lamp falling on the victim in the kitchen, and it relied on the testimony of the victim's eight-year-old daughter. Investigators found the brother-in-law and his wife living separately and recorded no specific act by either of them.

value: The victim's father and two of his sons were standing by a road when a tractor carrying several men stopped beside them. The men got down and, armed with axes, a sword, a dhariya and lathis, encircled the father and sons. The father and one son ran towards the village. The victim ran in another direction but was chased. One assailant caught hold of him and struck his head with an axe; after he fell, another assailant struck him again with an axe, and a third hit his right hand with a dhariya. According to the doctor who gave evidence, the victim died from haemorrhage and shock caused by the head injury, which damaged the brain and the carotid artery in the neck. The victim's brother was also attacked: he was caught, struck on the left temple with a dhariya and behind the ear with an axe, and hit on the face with a lathi, after which he became unconscious. He received four incised wounds and a fracture of the left parietal bone. The assailants left believing both were dead. The injured brother gave a detailed account of the incident. Two other eyewitnesses, who were related to him, described the same events and were found to be consistent on the main prosecution case. The parties had a prior dispute over land and an earlier murder. The accused examined defence witnesses.

value: A dispute arose after the victim allegedly stole a hen belonging to one of the accused. A community settlement was held and the victim paid a penalty, but the accused were reportedly still unhappy with it. Shortly afterwards, one accused allegedly confronted a witness about the matter and caused bleeding injuries to him, and the witness was examined by a doctor. On the following morning, the victim and this witness were summoned to a courtyard on the pretext of a meeting. On arrival, they were tied to a bamboo pole and a tree. Several accused, armed with lathis and tangies (sharp cutting weapons), allegedly beat the victim with lathis while the witness escaped. The victim was beaten to death. The victim's two wives, who had followed him to the courtyard, witnessed the assault. The first wife gave a statement to the police naming all accused as the assailants, and an investigation followed. The post-mortem doctor recorded fourteen injuries, mostly bruises and abrasions, including two rib fractures and haematoma under the scalp, stated that all injuries contributed to death, and said a blunt object such as a lathi could cause them. The witness, who was related to the victim, named his brother among the assailants. No witness attributed specific blows to specific accused, and the tangies were not used.

value: On 5 November 1990 a man unknown to the victim was looking for her house in a city and asked a passer-by for directions. The passer-by took him to a second woman, who escorted him to the victim's house. At about 1 p.m. a witness saw him at the victim's door. He said a relative was expected to come to the house; the victim replied that the relative had not arrived. That witness left before the man entered the house. That evening the victim did not come to a neighbour's house to watch television. The neighbour sent a child to call her, and the victim said relatives from her village had arrived and she had to cook for them. value: On 20 August 2006, at about 2 p.m., the victim, a 17-year-old girl who had taken goats to graze in a forest about half a kilometre from her village, was sitting alone on a footpath when the accused caught hold of her from behind. When she asked why, the accused did not respond. The accused physically abused her body, removed her clothes, made her lie on the ground and committed sexual assault by rape. She raised an alarm but no one came. After leaving, the accused threatened her with consequences if she disclosed the incident. Out of fear she did not tell her parents for several days, but remained tense and distressed. On 2 September 2006 she consumed poison, became unconscious and was taken to several hospitals, finally to a postgraduate institute, where she remained until 10 September 2006. On regaining consciousness she told her father and brother that the accused had raped her on 20 August. A first information report was registered on 11 September 2006, after which she was medically examined. The examining doctor recorded no fresh evidence of bleeding, tear or scratch over the vulva, only a slightly reddened area on the outer mucosa, and noted that the hymen was intact. The doctor also noted that the examination was carried out 21 days after the occurrence. The victim's age was established through a birth certificate, a matriculation certificate and medical age tests. The accused was arrested on 12 September 2006 and a charge sheet was filed. The victim's account was supported by her father and brother.

The prosecution case was that the accused and a co-accused killed the victim on the intervening night of 21/22 June 1995 at the instigation of the victim's wife, with whom the co-accused was alleged to have an illicit relationship, and that the body was thrown into the canal. The accused was alleged to have a grudge over the victim's marriage to the wife and a previous fight with the victim. A family member testified that the victim had been seen with the accused and the co-accused on 21 June 1995. A doctor testified that the victim had been murdered about one week before the post-mortem, which found grievous injuries to the neck and scalp and multiple skull fractures. Recoveries were made on the disclosure statements of the accused and the co-accused: the victim's chappal, and blood-stained shirt and trousers of the accused found in a polythene bag under a bridge. Further blood-stained clothing was recovered hidden near the village. The laboratory reported human blood on the clothes, and blood was also found on a hexa blade and the frame of a saw.

value: Some twenty years after an earlier family dispute, which had caused enmity between two families, a group of seventeen persons, including the two accused, allegedly assembled with the common object of killing the victim. An inspector went to the scene that night and recorded the statement of the victim's wife, and a first information report was registered the next morning. The post-mortem examination recorded fifteen incised wounds, mainly on the neck, chest, shoulder, arm and hand. The victim's two sons were also treated for cut injuries. The victim's wife testified that she had known both accused for a long time because they were closely related, and that she recognised them even though it was dark, relying on a street light and electricity supply at the scene. One injured son initially did not support the prosecution but, when examined, named the two accused as taking part in the attack. A wireman from the electricity board gave evidence that power was supplied at the scene at the relevant time. Recoveries were made on the basis of the accused's disclosure statements.

value: On the evening of 2 March 1991, the victim, a medical practitioner, was attending patients in a clinic when two unidentified youths shot the victim from point-blank range, and the victim died. A report of the incident was lodged the following day. During the investigation, several witnesses who had heard about the occurrence from the victim's wife and daughter were examined. The post-mortem examination recorded two bullet wounds, one on the right side of the face near the outer corner of the eye and one on the left side of the neck just below the ear, and gave shock and haemorrhage from the bullet injuries as the cause of death. The victim's daughter had been with the victim at the clinic and was an eyewitness, while the victim's wife was slightly away from the scene. The eyewitness gave a statement to the investigating officers about two years and eight months after the incident. He stated that he had been threatened by a co-accused. His acquaintance with the accused was a fortnight old when he accompanied the accused and another person to the clinic, where the other person went inside pretending to be a patient. He asserted that the accused fired at the victim, who fell and died. The accused was arrested about eight years after the incident, following the eyewitness's statement. The victim's wife and daughter were not examined as witnesses.

value: The victim, a doctor posted at a village dispensary, left his home by car in January 1997 carrying a briefcase and a wrist watch. Later that day a dispenser at the dispensary informed the victim's brother that the victim's body had been found in a field in a nearby village. The body lay on its side with multiple injuries from a sharp-edged weapon, blood was on the ground nearby, and the victim's car was missing. The victim's brother lodged a first information report and a post-mortem was conducted. The post-mortem surgeon recorded seven injuries, opined that death resulted from shock and haemorrhage, and stated that a kirpan could have caused the injuries. A co-accused, held by another police force in a separate matter, made statements implicating two other men. His first statement named a different accomplice who had taken only the watch and briefcase, and the car was recovered on his disclosure. In a later statement he named the two men, saying one took the briefcase and the other the watch. Following disclosures, the two men were arrested and a briefcase and wrist watch were recovered. The victim's wife identified the items as belonging to her husband, stating that the watch bore initials. The victim's brother testified that three men arrived at the victim's house shortly after the victim left, asked for him, and gave their names. No footprints were found in the kutcha area where the body lay, and no other evidence placed the two men near the scene.

value: On 25 March 1999, the victim and a companion withdrew four lakh rupees in cash from a bank and rode two-wheelers back toward their office. Near a market, a black scooter carrying two men approached from behind. The pillion rider fired a pistol at the victim, who fell from the scooter. The two men snatched the money bag, which also contained a cheque book, and turned back. When the companion tried to stop them, the pillion rider fired at him, injuring him. The assailants then fled on the scooter with the money bag. The victim died from a gunshot wound to the back, with severe haemorrhage and injury to vital organs. The companion received multiple gunshot wounds to the shoulder, neck, face and tongue and lost consciousness. The complainant, who was present, reported the incident promptly to the police, and officers visited the spot and recorded the death and injuries. The assailants were unknown to the complainant and the companion. Police could not trace the culprits for several years. In July 2006 a special team was formed, and police received information identifying the accused. A local resident, described as the Pradhan of his mohalla, stated that the accused had confessed to him. The accused were arrested at a naka in August 2006 when they were seen riding a scooter. The accused declined a test identification parade. The eyewitnesses later identified the accused at trial.

value: On 25 November 2003 the victim was found dead in the courtyard of a family house. The victim had been married into the household in July 2003. The prosecution case was that the step mother-in-law of the victim, who was annoyed with the victim over a domestic dispute, engaged three other persons to kill the victim. The only eyewitness was a thirteen-year-old domestic servant living in the house. According to the witness, one assailant held the victim while another stabbed the victim three to four times with a knife in the courtyard. The step mother-in-law was present in the passage, and a further person stood outside the house. After the assault, the assailants threatened the witness not to disclose anything. The witness was then taken to the terrace by the step mother-in-law and told to say that thieves had committed the crime. The step mother-in-law then began shouting and lay down near the victim. The victim's husband, returning from his clinic, found the servant weeping and the victim dead, and the step mother-in-law unconscious nearby. A First Information Report was lodged the same evening. Post-mortem examination recorded fourteen incised wounds, neurogenic and haemorrhagic shock as the cause of death, and a two-month pregnancy. Investigators seized a bloodstained knife, a hair found in the victim's grip, bloodstained cloth of the victim and of the step mother-in-law, and cement mortar. Three accused were arrested on 29 November 2003 and one on 22 December 2003. The witness identified the accused in test identification parades held within about a fortnight and four days of arrest, and identified them again in court.

value: On the anniversary of the couple's marriage, the accused and a co-accused were allegedly present in the house where the accused and the victim lived. At the hospital, a doctor examined the victim and recorded her statement that her husband had poured kerosene oil on her and ignited it, and a nurse attending her supported that account. A person who accompanied the victim's brother to the hospital testified that the victim had said in their presence that her husband had set her on fire. Neighbours heard a commotion and saw the victim near the gateway, as did a son of the accused from an earlier marriage. A maid servant present at the time could not be examined. value: The victim was married to the accused on 20 June 1995. On 1 March 1996, about nine months after the marriage, she suffered burn injuries. Her statement, recorded by a Chief Judicial Magistrate on 2 March 1996 after a medical fitness endorsement, had two parts. The first part described an accident in which a kerosene stove burst while she was preparing tea. The second part alleged that the accused had been pressing her to bring Rs. One lakh from her parents and had threatened to kill her. It further alleged that the accused had tried to hang her, had earlier tried to burn her at night, and at about 5.30 a.m. had doused her from behind with kerosene and set her alight. She stated that the first part had been tutored by the accused. A First Information Report was registered on the basis of that statement. The victim died on 12 March 1996. The post-mortem examination found superficial to deep burns over most of the body, excluding the face, scalp, both legs, feet and part of the left upper arm. The doctor recorded that the cause of death was ante mortem burns. He agreed that kerosene poured from behind would leave burns on the back, and that a stove burst would ordinarily have affected the face and scalp, which were not burnt. The victim's mother testified that the victim had told her of quarrels over a demand of Rs. One lakh for a piggery farm. The victim's father testified to the same demand and to physical abuse. A letter from the victim to her father demanding Rs. 5,000 was also in evidence. The accused was reported to have donated blood, but the victim died despite it. The case was then converted to a dowry-related offence and a charge sheet was filed.

value: The victim was attacked at a village temple by a large group of villagers at about dawn, after prayers, and was struck with a sword. The accused, part of the crowd, chased him from place to place, including to the homes of relatives, where relatives and others were also assaulted. The attackers removed roof tiles and tin sheets to reach him, dragged him into a field and assaulted him with swords, axes and a sattur. Houses in the area were damaged and some set on fire, and documents, gold ornaments and cash were taken or burnt. Family members took the victim to hospital, where he was found dead. The post-mortem recorded multiple chop and incised wounds, skull fractures and sub-dural haematoma, with the cause of death given as hemorrhage and shock due to multiple chop wounds with head injury. The victim's brother lodged a complaint naming thirty-four persons and attributing overt acts to some. The spot panchnama recorded blood stains at the temple, the well, a road and the houses. After disclosure statements by several accused, blood-stained weapons were recovered the day after the incident. At trial, most eye-witnesses, including close relatives, were declared hostile on identity. The sole eye-witness, the victim's wife, described the incident in stages and identified specific accused. Her account was said to be supported by the medical evidence and other material.

value: On the night of 27 June 1997, around 10:00 p.m., the victim, who was a village sarpanch, was sitting and talking with two other persons near a hotel in the village, with street lights on and a chimney burning nearby. Several men arrived at the spot. One carried a sword, another a farsa, another an axe, and the rest lathis. The man with the sword, while abusing the victim and saying he could not escape that day, struck the victim on the head, causing bleeding. Another assailant then struck the victim's head with the farsa, and a third struck the head with an axe, after which the victim fell. Others struck with lathis. Witnesses pleaded for the victim to be spared, and the assailants left after warning the victim not to contest against them in future. The injured eyewitness went to the police station about one kilometre away, and a first information report was registered at 10:45 p.m. The investigating officer visited the scene at 11:10 p.m. and prepared the crime details form. The injured eyewitness was sent for medical examination, completed by 1:30 a.m. The post mortem recorded eight injuries on the body, four of them grievous. The body was taken to the hospital by 7:30 a.m. the next day. Witnesses who came on hearing shouts corroborated the account. The accused were arrested on 28 June 1997, weapons were seized on 29 June 1997 at their instance, and disclosure statements were recorded. The express report was received by the magistrate only on 30 June 1997.

Chemical examination of the viscera detected organo chloro insecticide and ethyl alcohol. The victim's brother, father and uncle testified that the victim had complained of taunts and torture over dowry. One witness said that at a post-marriage ceremony an accused complained that the marriage expenses had not been recovered. The victim had complained to the family twice about dowry demands. The victim's brother said no dowry demand was made before the marriage. The defence contended that the victim had swallowed poison and then set herself on fire. Police investigated, and a charge-sheet was filed against all four accused.

value: On the night of 11 January 2000, the victim was last known to be travelling from a town toward his village after an outing. Around 10 p.m., the victim's brother saw the accused near a tubewell and a bus stand, running away with blood-stained clothes; the brother identified the accused in vehicle headlights and did not then know of any killing. The next morning the victim's wife reported that he had not returned home. The family searched and found the victim's body near a water-supply tubewell, lying in a pool of blood, with wounds on the forehead, nose and eyebrows; his shirt, sweater and slippers lay some distance away. Police recorded the body's location, took possession of the body, a blood-stained brick and clothing, and prepared an inquest. A post-mortem recorded multiple injuries, including contusions on the back, a large chest swelling with fractured ribs and blood in the chest cavity, and lacerated wounds on the forehead and above the right eye; the examining doctors stated that these injuries were sufficient to cause death. In the early hours of the next day the accused attended a government hospital, where a doctor recorded a superficial incised wound on the back of the left forearm with a corresponding cut in the shirt. Later, a witness stated that the accused had told him that on the earlier night he had quarrelled with the victim after both drank liquor and had struck him with a brick. On disclosure by the accused, police recovered blood-stained clothes concealed in a wooden box in the accused's house. Forensic analysis found the same blood group ('O') on the recovered clothes and on the victim's clothing.

value: The prosecution alleges a conspiracy to secure admission to undergraduate medical courses for candidates who had not earned places on merit. Each candidate reportedly paid several lakh rupees to middlemen, who shared the money with officials. The accused is alleged to have received money from candidates through a general manager of an institution connected with the accused, who handled admissions. During investigation, the general manager made a disclosure that led to the recovery of money and documents, including a seizure of cash. Seized material included a list of candidates sponsored from the accused's institution, electronic data from an examination board office, documents and activity charts from that board, and memoranda of other accused persons. A statement recorded under the criminal procedure code by a parent of a candidate said the accused had asked him to meet the general manager and pay a sum for admission, which he could not pay. The investigation involved a large number of accused persons, a substantial number of whom had been arrested, with further charge sheets pending.

value: On the evening of 1 April 1983, the victim was struck with a stone at about 8.30 pm in a village. About four days earlier, during a festival, the victim had visited the accused's home. Later that night the accused came to the victim's household to assault the victim, alleging that the victim's family had been involved in an incident of knocking at the door of a woman in the accused's household at night with evil intention. Family members intervened, preventing the accused from dragging the victim out, and the accused left with a threat. The victim did not return home that night. The next morning a witness said he had seen the victim with the accused at about 7.30 pm, and two eyewitnesses said they saw the accused beating the victim with a stone at about 8.30 pm. Another witness said he had seen the two together just before the incident. The victim's body was later found near a riverbank. The post-mortem recorded that the face and head were flattened, with multiple irregular lacerated wounds, a disfigured face, pulverized skull and mandible bones, and brain matter flowing from the wounds. The death was attributed to shock and haemorrhage from ante-mortem injuries which could have been caused by a stone between 8 and 9 pm. The accused was examined and had three injuries to the face, which the doctor said were caused by a hard blunt object or friction about a day earlier. The accused said he had been falsely implicated because of complaints he had made against local officials.

value: The proprietor of a multi-storied hotel and adjoining club in Indore obtained a building permission in 1993, valid for one year, with renewal required before a set date. A revised building plan was later submitted to the Building Officer, who approved it along with a renewal of the permission, and a completion certificate for the adjoining club was granted shortly afterwards. The prosecution alleged that the revised plan was a complete departure from the original plan, with the built-up area of the hotel increased substantially and that of the club's ground floor decreased markedly. It was alleged that the revision was sanctioned without approval from the high-rise building committee and without electricity, water supply, sewage and fire-safety clearances. It was further alleged that the completion certificate was issued only seven days after the revision of the permission, although the club could not plausibly have been completed with all compliances within that time. A Sub-Engineer in the building permission branch was alleged to have made notings in the note sheet favouring the proprietor. It was alleged that the Building Officer received free lifetime honorary membership of the club for himself and five family members as illegal gratification. The Building Officer was also alleged to have failed to inform the property tax department about the completion certificate, leading to alleged tax evasion of Rs.5,49,000. An anti-corruption agency registered a first information report in January 1998 and, after investigation, filed a charge-sheet against the three accused.

value: The victim, a widow who ran a beauty parlour, had become acquainted with one of the accused, and the two developed a close friendship; that accused frequently visited the victim's home and sometimes stayed overnight there. The tenant later saw the accused return alone around 10 to 10:30 p.m. and, when asked about the victim, was told the victim was engaged with someone and would be brought back later. A school official testified that no function had been scheduled at that school on that date. The next morning the victim's body was found in an isolated jungle about 25 km from the residence, with the neck tied by one end of a saree whose other end was tied to a tree. The post-mortem found lacerated head wounds sufficient to cause death, and an injury consistent with forcible intercourse. Investigators arrested the accused, and on the basis of a confessional statement by one accused a motorcycle was seized. Recoveries of an improvised pipe gun with wooden butts were made from near a river and the jungle, and blood was detected on the butts. Call records showed numerous calls between the accused, and a notebook belonging to a co-accused contained a coded number of one accused. A witness testified that one accused threatened him and another witness not to disclose anything to the police.

value: At about 9.30 p.m. on the evening in question, the victim and a companion were riding a scooter near a sweet-meat shop when several persons attacked them. The rider lost control and both fell. The attackers then assaulted the victim: some stabbed him repeatedly with knives, while others beat him with iron rods. One attacker tried to stab the companion but missed, and another stabbed the companion in the left arm. The companion escaped and hid in a nearby office. Two persons returning from work saw the incident and took the injured victim to a government hospital. The companion also returned to the scene and was taken to hospital, where his statement was recorded and a case was registered. The victim was later moved to another hospital. A magistrate recorded the victim's dying declaration after confirming through the treating doctor that he was conscious; the declaration named several attackers. The victim died three days after the attack. The post-mortem examination found five stab injuries at different parts of the body and attributed death to multiple stab wounds. The investigating officer later arrested several suspects and recovered four knives and two iron rods on their instructions. The prosecution case was that the victim had been attacked because he had been a witness in an earlier murder case in which one of the attackers had been an accused.

value: On a morning in January 1984, a group of men including the accused came to the house of the victim's family armed with lathis, a farsa and handmade bombs. They began abusing the family and threatened that they would not leave the family alive. One of the accused allegedly hurled a handmade bomb at a family member, causing leg injuries, and another accused threw a handmade bomb onto the chest of the victim, who suffered serious burn and laceration injuries. Other accused used lathis, and a farsa was used to injure a woman on her hand. The victim, who was declared brought dead at hospital, was the subject of a post-mortem examination, which recorded extensive burns and lacerated wounds on the chest and hand and found the death homicidal, caused by an explosive substance. Several family members who were present were also injured and were examined by a doctor, and their injuries were proved by medical reports. The complainant lodged a First Information Report shortly after the incident. The investigating officer prepared a spot map, collected bloodstained soil, and seized the lathis, the farsa and the handmade bombs at the instance of the accused. Several other persons who were present were not examined as witnesses. The accused gave a version that the complainant's side had confined a man who later died.

value: The victim had been married to the accused only a short time before the incident, and the couple lived in a rented house near the victim's parental home. Both earned a living through daily wage work. On the morning of the incident, the victim went out to answer a call of nature and, on returning somewhat late, was questioned by the accused, who suspected her of infidelity. Despite her attempts to explain, the accused began assaulting her with fists and kicks. He then poured kerosene from a nearby lamp over her and set her ablaze. Her saree caught fire and she ran towards the accused, whose hands were burnt. When she screamed for help, the accused poured water on her. Neighbours and her parents gathered and she was taken to hospital. On the way, she told her mother, sister-in-law and a neighbour what had happened. The neighbour testified only that she said the accused had beaten and kicked her, and did not support the account of kerosene. A sub-inspector recorded her statement at the hospital, on which a First Information Report was registered. After a doctor certified her mental fitness, an executive magistrate recorded a dying declaration naming the accused as the person who poured kerosene and set her on fire. She succumbed to burn injuries on 12 September 2005. The post-mortem found death due to shock and septicaemia caused by 60% burn injuries. A panch witness spoke to a kerosene lamp prepared in an empty liquor bottle in the house. The accused's defence was that the fire was accidental and that he had tried to extinguish it.

value: On a morning in September 1996, near a cycle stand inside a college campus, a group of seven accused, some armed with lathis, knives and khukris, approached two students standing there. They asked the victim and a second student to withdraw their names from a college election. When both refused, the accused assaulted them with their weapons. The victim was struck on the back, neck and face, then ran from the spot, became entangled in wire fencing near a nearby building, and fell. Several accused chased him there and attacked him again with sticks. The second student suffered a head injury. About three hundred students gathered. The victim was taken to hospital and died the next day. The second student lodged a written complaint at a police station, and the shirt he wore was seized. A medical officer examined both injured persons. The victim's frontal bone was found fractured and a lung ruptured; the second student's injuries were consistent with sticks. Eyewitnesses named all the accused and described their individual roles. One witness who had been present gave differing accounts to police and in court. The weapons were not recovered, and a blood-stained shirt was recovered six days after the incident.

value: The victim was riding home from work on a bicycle at about 8:00 p.m. on the evening of the incident, with his younger brother following about 10 to 15 feet behind. The brother ran home to alert the family, and relatives came to the scene before the victim was taken to hospital. Before dying, the victim gave two statements, one recorded at the hospital by a police officer and one recorded by an Executive Magistrate after a doctor certified he was conscious. Both named the persons involved and described the group's role and an earlier enmity with the main assailants. The brother testified as an eyewitness. After investigation, a charge sheet was filed against ten persons and twenty prosecution witnesses were examined.

value: The prosecution alleged that the accused had a long-running dispute with the victim's family over the sale of a plot of land and the flow of irrigation water from a distributary, and that they demanded that the land be transferred to them and later demanded money for letting water flow. The victim's brother and mother said they witnessed the assault from a nearby field. The brother said he moved to intervene but his mother dissuaded him. After the assailants left, the brother and mother went near the injured man but returned home. Later they went back to the field with the victim's father, who found the victim with his hands still tied, a leg injury and his eyes burning from chilly powder. The father went to lodge a report at a police post. A Sub-Inspector arrived at about 10.00 p.m. in a police jeep and recorded a written complaint from the brother as the first information, in which the victim was described as dead. The brother was then directed to untie the victim's hands, and the victim was taken to hospital, where he was found to have died on the way. value: At a farewell party at an army unit's barracks, drinks were served. The accused became involved in a heated argument with a senior non-commissioned officer, who slapped the accused. The accused then fought with and abused that officer and also abused the victim, a fellow soldier, who had tried to intervene. An officer intervened and directed two junior soldiers to escort the accused to his living barracks. Later, the victim was found lying on the floor of the room, bleeding from the mouth and nose, with a stab wound to the chest. The accused was found lying on a bed in the same room. Witnesses testified that no one other than the accused and the victim had been present in the room, and that the accused had been seen leaving quietly through the rear door. The accused was absent from the morning fall-in parade. At about 1.30 to 2 a.m., the accused surrendered at a nearby police station and said he had stabbed a person with a knife. Unit officers went to the station, and the accused confessed to stabbing the victim. The forensic surgeon who conducted the autopsy found two ante mortem injuries, one a deep stab wound to the chest that could have caused death. The knife was not recovered. A statement the accused gave during a summary of evidence under the army rules, describing a scuffle and saying he stabbed the victim to free his neck, was proved through the officer who recorded it, with a supporting witness. The adjutant lodged an FIR and the accused was handed to military police.

value: The victim lived in a joint family with a spouse and in-laws after marriage and had a young daughter. Within about two years of marriage, the victim was allegedly tortured by the spouse and in-laws over demands for dowry and for work performance, and was driven out of the matrimonial home. The victim repeatedly left and stayed at shelters and other places, and was returned to the matrimonial home after mediation by relatives. The victim reported demands for Rs.20,000 and filed a maintenance claim, which went unpaid, and lodged a criminal complaint alleging cruelty and dowry harassment. Several witnesses, including the victim's paternal uncle, that uncle's wife, the victim's brother, a social worker and neighbours, testified that the victim was regularly taunted and physically harassed, that the victim was seen sleeping at odd places, and that heated quarrels took place. One witness said the victim came to him for help, claiming the in-laws were trying to kill her, and had burn marks on her hands. On the day of the incident, the victim ran out of the house calling for help, and one in-law described the condition as epileptic fits. The victim was later found to have consumed poisonous tablets. The accused were in the house at the time and took the victim to hospital when the condition became critical. In a dying declaration, the victim stated the tablets were taken by mistake, and the examining doctor recorded that the victim was stable and conscious enough to give a statement. The victim died. A relative lodged a complaint with the police, after which the scene was examined in a panchanama, witness statements were recorded and the accused were arrested.

value: The victim, who is blind and illiterate, lived in her family home with her brothers after her mother left. The accused, a friend of one of the victim's brothers, began visiting the house and talking with the victim. The prosecution case is that about a year before the incident the accused came to the house when the victim was alone, said he loved her and would marry her, and wanted intercourse. The victim tried to avoid it because she was blind, but she submitted after being assured of marriage and support. The accused then came to the house whenever the victim was alone and had intercourse with her. When the victim became pregnant and asked him to marry her, he stopped visiting. The incident was disclosed to the victim's father, who called a village Panchayat. There the accused admitted having had intercourse with the victim but refused to marry her and left. The prosecution's case is that, though blind, the victim could recognise the accused by voice and touch. The matter was investigated, the victim was medically examined, and a charge-sheet was filed. Prosecution witnesses included the victim, a doctor who gave the medical examination report, a radiologist whose X-ray examination estimated the victim's age at approximately 18 years, and persons who attended the Panchayat. The victim testified that she recognised the accused by his voice, that he committed intercourse with her on the pretext of marriage, and that he stopped visiting after she became pregnant. She also testified that the Panchayat was held after she disclosed the incident.

value: On a Saturday afternoon in August 1995, the victim was sitting in a pandal set up for a festival, talking with a person who was the decoration contractor for the pandal. Two unknown persons entered the pandal from a road, were allegedly escorted by three other persons, and opened fire on the victim, firing many bullets into his head, chest and other parts of his body at point blank range. The firing created commotion in the pandal. The contractor tried to run, was hit by a bullet and fell down. The assailants escaped. The victim was taken to hospital and declared dead on arrival. The first information report was lodged about an hour and a quarter later by an eyewitness who said he saw the incident from the first floor gallery of a building abutting the pandal. Five eyewitnesses later gave evidence, including the injured contractor. Several witnesses said they identified suspects in test identification parades, which were held roughly a year or more after the incident. The prosecution also relied on recovery of a weapon and a ballistic report. The post-mortem report recorded no injury on the victim's forehead, and the victim had been attacked from behind.

value: The victim, an 18-year-old, was alone at home in the late evening on 4 March 1989. The victim's parents had gone out, and the victim's brother and sister had gone to watch an evening movie. At about 9.30 pm the brother returned and found the victim on fire in bushes near the house. He smothered the flames with a quilt and took the victim on a push-cart to the Rural Hospital, where no doctor was available. A waterman and a maid-servant cleaned the wounds and administered intravenous saline. A police sub-inspector arrived at once and recorded an oral statement from the victim, which bore the victim's thumb impression. In it the victim said the accused, with whom the victim had a love affair and who the victim said had made the victim pregnant, had been asked to marry the victim that evening. The victim said the accused then poured kerosene on the victim and set the victim alight with a match-stick. On the police requisition, an Executive Magistrate recorded a dying declaration at the hospital in the presence of two hospital employees, and the victim put a thumb impression on it. The victim was then moved to a district hospital. On 5 March 1989 another Executive Magistrate recorded a different statement, attributing the burns to a falling chimney lamp while the victim slept. That statement had no thumb impression. The victim died on 9 March 1989. A medical officer conducted the autopsy and recorded about 72 per cent burns. The defence case was that the burns were accidental.

value: The victim, a 15-year-old girl, was an enrolled member of a lawn tennis association whose office was in a garage of a house owned by the accused, who was the association's president and a senior police officer. The accused had told the victim's father that he would arrange special coaching for her at the association, and he asked that she come to his office. On the day in question, the victim and a companion went to the office at the accused's request. The accused asked the companion to fetch the coach, and she left the room. On returning, the companion saw the accused holding one of the victim's hands while his other arm was around her waist and he was pulling her towards his chest to embrace her, while the victim tried to push him back with her free hand. On seeing the companion, the accused released the victim and sat down. The companion later found the victim crying and the victim described what had happened. The two girls initially decided not to tell their parents, fearing the accused's position. On a later date the victim disclosed the incident to her parents, and a memorandum describing the incident, signed by the victim and others, was submitted to state authorities. A state official conducted an enquiry and recorded statements. The victim's signature on the memorandum was disputed, and a handwriting expert was examined; several witnesses testified that they saw the victim sign it. The victim's father testified that the accused had visited him on an earlier day, asked that the victim not be sent abroad, and asked that she come to his office; the companion's account was consistent with this. The ball picker and the coach were not examined. A formal FIR was later registered and the investigation was carried out by the CBI, which filed a charge-sheet.

value: The victim's cattle allegedly strayed into the fields of neighbouring residents in the morning and damaged a standing crop. The neighbours abused the victim, who drove the cattle back home. In the early afternoon, the victim was sitting in his compound with his brother, a second witness and a third witness, when a dispute broke out between him and neighbours who lived next door over the same issue. The exchanges grew heated and the neighbours, including the accused, allegedly closed in on the victim. On being urged by another neighbour to eliminate the victim, one of the accused allegedly fetched a gun and fired at the victim, who fell injured. The other accused then allegedly struck him with sticks. The victim's brother and two witnesses who tried to intervene were allegedly stopped by the gun being pointed at them. The victim died at the spot. The first information report was lodged at about 3.15 p.m. the same day. Investigation included an inquest, a sketch map of the scene, and collection of blood-stained earth, which a chemical analyst found to be human blood. Three eyewitnesses testified to the sequence of events and identified the accused. The post-mortem doctor recorded firearm wounds on the head, chest and right upper arm, multiple abrasions and contusions, and death from shock and haemorrhage. The doctor also recorded simple lacerated or incised wounds and contusions on some of the accused. The defence contended that the accused had been attacked while escorting cattle and that one of them fired in self-defence.

value: The accused and the victim had been married for several years and had two sons. The accused had earlier left police service and worked abroad for a period, sending money home. On the evening of the incident, the accused and the victim returned from a short spiritual retreat. The victim was sent home with the accused's son while the accused went looking for labourers. Later that evening, the accused's brother suffered an epileptic attack at a tea shop, and the accused asked two men to fetch the brother's medical papers from the house. They found the front door open, a lamp lit, and no response from the victim. On entering, they found the victim hanging from a hook in the work area by a saree, with movements, and they raised an alarm. Others arrived, and the saree was cut with a knife and the body brought down. The victim was taken to hospital and declared dead. The prosecution alleged that the accused smothered and strangled the victim with a plastic rope and then hanged her. A nylon rope and broken glass bangles were recovered from under a cot in the dining room, away from the hanging site. The chemical report found no blood on the rope, and the hairs on it could not be attributed to a sex. The post-mortem doctor recorded pressure abrasion on the neck, a fracture of the hyoid bone, and forehead and facial injuries, but could not say whether death was from suicidal or homicidal hanging. The accused's account was that two unknown persons pushed the accused down on the way home that evening. Three witnesses gave statements at the inquest, and were re-examined nearly four years later, shortly before the charge-sheet was submitted.

value: Two adjacent households, whose members were brothers, had a long-running dispute over land. On the day in question, the son of one household was working in the fields when the accused hurled abuses at him. The son returned home upset and complained to his father. The father went to the rooftop of his house and called the accused over. The accused came with his own son. When the father asked why the accused had abused his son, the accused replied angrily that he was justified and would continue. The accused then ran downstairs, fetched a double-barrelled 12-bore gun and fired at the father, striking him on the side of the head. It was alleged that the accused's son urged the firing. Hearing the commotion, the father's wife and two friends of the son rushed to the rooftop. The accused fired at them. One friend was struck in the abdomen and died, the father's wife was struck in the abdomen, and the other friend was struck in the mouth and head. The injured were taken to hospital, where the friend who was struck died. The accused and his son then fled. In the investigation, the 12-bore gun loaded with two live cartridges was recovered from the accused, and four cartridge shells were recovered from the spot. The site plan prepared by the investigating officer matched the eyewitnesses' account of the place of occurrence. The eyewitnesses included the father and the injured. The medical evidence showed injuries on the deceased and the injured compatible with the weapon used.

value: The victim, who was involved in real estate, was contacted by phone by a caller offering a land deal, and over several weeks the callers built his confidence in the proposal. On the morning of the planned meeting, the victim went to the site in his own car. Several men arrived in a Honda City car; one pointed a revolver at him, his cell phone, car keys and cash were taken, his face was covered, his mouth was taped and his hands were tied, and he was forced into the dicky of the Honda City car. For about two days he was held captive and moved between places. He was chained, blindfolded and given drugs, and he heard his captors address each other by nicknames. The captors repeatedly phoned his father demanding ransom, first Rs. 5 crores and later Rs. 1 crore, threatening that the victim and family would be killed if it was not paid. The father raised money from several lenders, some of whom had marked packets of notes with initials. Money was thrown from a moving train as instructed, and the victim was released. Police registered an FIR, arrested the accused and, on their disclosure statements, recovered cash, firearms, the Honda City car, and the victim's driving licence and tape from the car's dicky. Telephone call records were collected, but no certificate was obtained for them. No identification parade was held. The victim identified the accused in later testimony.

value: The victim, a married woman, was sleeping in the matrimonial house in the early hours of 20 September 1999 when the accused persons came to her room. According to the victim's statement, the husband and his younger brother had earlier beaten her. Two other family members held her arms, the husband sprinkled kerosene on her and the brother lit a matchstick, setting her ablaze. Neighbours extinguished the fire. The accused persons took the victim to a hospital, where she was found to have about 100% burns. The attending doctor certified that she was fit to make a statement. A judicial magistrate then recorded her statement in the presence of the medical officer, and the doctor again certified that she remained fit during the recording. The victim died within a few hours. A post-mortem found the burns to be ante mortem and sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course. Following a disclosure by the husband, police recovered an empty plastic kerosene container. The victim's father and brother, examined as witnesses, did not support the prosecution account. The brother said the husband had been with him at his house on the night of the incident and that they learned of the burns at about 4 a.m. Hospital records showed that the husband had brought the victim to hospital and had her admitted. The victim's statement also alleged years of dowry demands and repeated beatings by the in-laws.

value: The victim was found hanging by a rope from the roof of a shed adjacent to the victim's house, and the victim's brother reported the death to police as unnatural. The sole eyewitness, a relative of both the victim and the accused, testified that on the night of the incident he returned from a village video show with the accused, who had been drinking. He said that when the victim was returning from relieving himself, the accused struck the victim twice from behind, sat on the victim's chest and pressed the victim's neck, while the co-accused covered the victim's mouth until the victim suffocated. He stated that the accused then tied a rope around the victim's neck and suspended the body from the shed roof, and threatened him with death if he disclosed the incident. He said the events lasted about an hour and that he raised no alarm. He disclosed the incident to three other persons about three days later. The investigating officer's spot map recorded no source of light in the locality. The post-mortem examination found death was due to asphyxia from constriction of the neck and not hanging by rope. The prosecution also relied on the victim's mother's evidence that she had rebuked the accused persons for secret talks between them. The case was initially registered as unnatural death and converted to murder six days later on the basis of disclosures by the eyewitness and three others.

value: The victim, a student, stayed overnight in a shed at a tube-well in a field, where electric light was available for his studies. At about 7.30 p.m., two relatives of the victim, carrying meals for him, met a third villager who wanted to irrigate his fields, and the three walked to the tube-well together. Near the tube-well they heard the sound of a gunshot from inside the shed. They hurried to the spot and saw four men come out of the shed. Two carried pistols, one carried a ballam and one carried a lathi. On seeing the witnesses, the men ran away. The witnesses found the victim lying dead in a pool of blood. They identified the men by an electric bulb on the shed roof and by torchlight. A report was prepared on the spot with the help of the victim's uncle and an FIR was lodged at the police station the same night. Investigators recorded witness statements, prepared a panchanama and sketch map, and collected blood-stained and unstained earth and two cartridges from the spot. The post-mortem found eight gunshot entry wounds on the right side of the neck and no blackening or scorching around the wound. The doctor opined that death was caused by gunshot injury. There was enmity between the accused's family and the victim's uncle's family arising from an earlier murder case in which the uncle had faced prosecution.

value: The incident occurred in the afternoon at the office of a third person, which had been arranged as a meeting to settle a dispute over the sale of a property, through a property dealer, between the accused and one of the victims. The victim, his two brothers and a witness were already present when the accused arrived with his father and another man. Witnesses gave two versions of what followed. One witness said that as soon as the deceased got up, the accused took out a revolver and fired at him, after which the accused's father also fired at the victim's brothers. Another witness said that the three brothers and the accused were involved in a scuffle in which the deceased and his brothers tried to strangulate the accused. The accused then reached for his revolver, the deceased released him and turned to run, and the accused fired. The bullet entered below the right shoulder of the deceased from the back and did not exit. A doctor stated that the shot was fired from a distant range, with no blackening, tattooing or charring. Seven bullets were fired and no empty cartridge cases were found at the scene. Two .32 revolvers were recovered, one from the accused and one from his father, but ballistic examination could not link the bullets to the accused's revolver. Two brothers died from gunshot wounds and a third brother was injured. Several witnesses gave differing accounts of who fired which shot.

value: The victim, a practising advocate, was in a car with his brother and an employee when about ten to twelve men attacked it. The assailants were reported to be armed with swords, daatars, a baseball bat and similar weapons. They smashed the front, back and driver's side windows of the car. The victim, seated inside, was struck on the head and bent away, suffering a blow to his right arm. The victim's brother opened the car door to escape, was struck on the head, and suffered finger injuries when he raised his hands to protect himself. He was then chased and injured further. Bystanders gathered after shouting, and the assailants left in their vehicles. The brother drove the injured men to hospital. Medical examination recorded that one injury to each of the two men was grievous and caused by a sharp-edged weapon, with other injuries simple. The employee sustained four simple injuries. During investigation, eleven persons were arrested and the weapons and vehicles used were recovered at their instance. Call detail records and CCTV footage from a nearby bank were analysed. The complainant alleged that the attack was carried out at the instance of a person against whom he had instituted several cases.

value: The victim, the newly elected chairman of a temple trust board, had proposed transferring a senior temple official and his associates, who feared exposure of financial irregularities. The victim was last seen on a afternoon in a blue car with one of the accused, leaving the temple premises. Witnesses who initially said they saw the victim leave the temple later turned hostile, though the court weighed their admissible parts together with other testimony. According to the prosecution, the accused took the victim to another temple complex, where a call girl was procured through a co-accused, the victim was sedated and then strangled. Cellular records showed a co-accused in contact with the person who brought the woman. A burnt, unidentified body was later found in a ditch in a neighbouring State the next day. Following a disclosure by one of the accused, the body was identified through a key tied with cotton thread matching the victim's room lock, gold dental caps, and DNA comparison with a blood sample from the victim's sister. A post-mortem recorded death by asphyxia from strangulation and homicide. The car used was later found burnt in a garage, and an insurance claim for it was rejected after a surveyor found no accidental or mechanical cause for the burning. A disclosure by another accused led police to the crime location, where a panchnama recorded the discovery of the room and of tablets.

value: On the evening of 10 March 1993, a group gathered at a road junction where an opposing political party had a presence, searching for supporters of that party travelling in passing buses. The victim was travelling in a stage carriage bus that stopped at the junction. Several persons boarded the bus, pulled the victim out, and took him to the front of the bus, where he was attacked. One of the attackers inflicted a stab wound on the back of the left side of the victim's chest and then two more stab wounds. When the victim tried to stand up, the other attackers beat him with a reaper and sticks. The victim was later found unconscious and bleeding on the road margin and was taken to hospital, where he was declared dead. The informant's statement was recorded at midnight and a first information report was registered. The autopsy recorded 26 injuries, with the cause of death given as multiple injuries to the chest. A stab wound of about 7.5 cm entered the left chest cavity and was stated to be sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. An independent resident who was travelling in the same bus described the attack, and another resident who lived nearby gave evidence naming further participants. A knife was identified in evidence. The informant, another eyewitness and the bus driver turned hostile, and several attesting witnesses to the seizure also turned hostile.

value: A land dispute between closely related families had strained relations after the victim cultivated land that had been leased to a relative. On the evening of 15 September 1994, the victim's wife, while cutting grass in her field, saw the three accused working in a nearby field and heard them say they would not spare the victim because he had beaten a relative. The accused left the field carrying an iron rod and twigs, and the wife followed them to a place where a relative was sitting injured on the road and the victim was standing nearby. The prosecution case was that one accused struck the victim on the head with an iron rod and stabbed him on the cheek, while the others beat his legs and hands with twigs. The accused then threw their weapons away and left. The victim was taken to a government hospital by the wife and another person and was declared dead. A post-mortem recorded six serious bleeding injuries to the scalp. Police registered a complaint from the wife and, separately, a case based on the injured relative's statement. Bloodstained iron rod, twigs and earth were seized. The accused were arrested on 17 September 1994 from a bus-stand, when blood-stained clothing worn by one accused was seized. All material objects were sent for chemical analysis.

value: In December 1980, a large number of people who had bought country liquor from a single licensed liquor vend in a village and consumed it fell seriously ill. Thirty-six of them died and forty-four lost their eyesight permanently. Post-mortem examinations of the deceased found methyl alcohol in their viscera. Doctors who examined the surviving victims attributed their loss of vision to intake of methyl alcohol. Statements made by the victims immediately after they fell ill, and by close relatives of the deceased, consistently identified the vend as the source of the liquor. Police produced and sealed bottles of the liquor from victims, and after the accused were interrogated they recovered empty bottles and corks used for preparing and storing the liquor. The vend's records were seized and were found to have been forged. The prosecution case was that the accused, as contractors of the licensed vend, adulterated liquor with methyl alcohol and sold it through their agents, knowing its toxic effect. After the tragedy received media coverage, the accused's staff were said to have thrown remaining bottles into a river and canal. Some bottles recovered from the canal were not tested for methyl alcohol, and the investigation was criticised for lapses.

value: The victim was married to the accused in January 1998 and died within about three years of the marriage, along with her young child, by drowning in a river. The prosecution case was that after the marriage the accused and other in-laws repeatedly beat and taunted the victim for bringing insufficient dowry and demanded a Maruti car or two lakh rupees. The victim's father testified that the victim told him about the maltreatment and that he gave the victim a fixed deposit receipt for thirty thousand rupees and spoke to the accused by phone. The victim's elder sister testified that on 16 February 2001 the victim visited her home, wept, complained of cruelty and said the accused had beaten her the previous night after she tried to stop him abusing her father; the victim's daughter was present. The same day the victim telephoned her father from a public call office, saying she had been maltreated, thrown out of the house, and would not be allowed back without a car or two lakh rupees. The operator at the call office and another witness saw the victim weeping during the call but could not hear the conversation. The post-mortem doctor estimated that about twelve days had elapsed between death and the post-mortem, placing the death on 16 or 17 February 2001. The victim's body and the child's body were found secured together with one chunni. The FIR was lodged on 17 February 2001.

value: The victim, a woman whose husband had died about eleven years earlier, lived in a joint family house with her son, her daughter and the accused, her brother-in-law. On the evening of 23 August 2007, the accused came to the house in a drunken state, abused the victim and her children and threatened to kill them. An elderly woman in the house took the son into an adjoining room and bolted it from outside, and sent the daughter to the house of the victim's maternal uncle. From the room's window, the son heard the victim crying out and saw the accused taking her towards the house of another person. Hours later, the accused opened the door and told the son that the victim had run away, and told him to tell the maternal uncle the same. Under threat from the accused and another person, the son told the uncle so. The uncle came to the house in the early hours of 24 August, and the son and uncle reported the victim missing at the police station. On 25 August the uncle received a call that the victim's body was hanging from a tree in a forest. The body was found hanging from a pine branch, a plastic rope tied around the neck. The autopsy surgeon found death due to haemorrhagic shock from a ruptured spleen, with anti-mortem injuries suggesting gagging, and found hanging was after death. The accused was taken into custody on 25 August. His confession on 27 August led to recovery of a lady's shirt from a room under construction. The sister-in-law testified that the victim had told her of ill-treatment by the accused, including an earlier beating and a compromise, and that the accused was a chronic drunkard. The accused did not report the victim missing to the police and gave no explanation for her death.

value: On a night in late July 2011, a group of friends gathered at a house for a drink party arranged at the behest of the victim, a 22-year-old man. During the gathering the victim, while smoking, blew smoke into the face of the accused. The accused objected that the victim was junior in age and should not smoke in the accused's presence. A sudden physical fight followed, and the accused struck the victim with a knife six times on different parts of the body. Two friends who were present as eyewitnesses testified that, after realising the victim was badly injured, the accused offered water and took the victim to hospital with other friends. The accused stayed at the hospital until the victim died. The accused also telephoned the victim's father and asked him to come to the hospital. Eyewitnesses stated that doctors did not give immediate treatment but insisted on first calling the father. Police received a telephone message about a quarrel near a tunnel and an injured person being taken to hospital. The Station House Officer recorded the statement of the victim's father under section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The knife was recovered at the accused's instance, and the nature of the injuries was attributed to the same knife. Four persons who had gathered at the house were proceeded against, and three of them were later separated from the case. The victim died from the knife injuries.

value: On the evening of 19 June 1995, an altercation reportedly took place between the victim and one of the accused over a sum of money, near a grocery shop in the village; the victim was said to have slapped that accused during the scuffle. Later that evening, a group of about sixteen persons, armed with sticks, a sword, an axe and an iron pipe, allegedly entered the victim's house, dragged him out, and assaulted his hands and legs. The assault allegedly continued while he was dragged along the road and to a field, where his right palm was reportedly cut off. The victim's wife, who witnessed part of the incident, reportedly hid in a cattle shed for about two hours before informing a neighbour, and a complaint was lodged the following day. The victim's body was found in a field on 21 June 1995 without the right palm, which was found at some distance. value: On the day in question, the victim had finished a meal at home, and then stepped into the courtyard to drink water. One accused, who had a rivalry with the victim, came into the courtyard carrying an axe. Several other accused stood at the door of a neighbouring house; some were armed with rifles and one with a stick. The first accused urged the others to kill the victim and then struck the victim with the axe. The victim ran out of the courtyard, but four men at the neighbouring door caught hold of the victim. The victim's mother came to shield the victim and was injured near her ear when she tried to take the axe away. The accused armed with a rifle fired at the victim, and the shot hit the victim's back, causing the victim to fall. The first accused is said to have taken a gun from a third accused and also fired at the victim. When villagers arrived, all the accused fled the spot. The post-mortem found one circular gunshot wound of 1.5 cm on the back, in the middle of the spine, with a fractured spinal bone and five pellets recovered from the spinal cord; the doctor opined that this injury was sufficient to cause death. The investigating officer seized a .12 bore cartridge, an empty cartridge and two plastic pieces smelling of gunpowder under a seizure memo. Eyewitnesses, including the victim's wife, father and two neighbours, gave consistent accounts that the rifle-armed accused was present. The first accused was arrested and, on his statement, an axe was recovered. None of the witnesses could say which part of the victim's body was hit by the shot fired by the third accused.

value: The victim married the accused in May 1991. The victim's father alleged that after the marriage the victim was mistreated by her husband, father-in-law, mother-in-law and sister-in-law because they demanded dowry. The father said he gave dowry beyond his means, gave a gold chain about a year after the marriage, and paid cash sums on later occasions, but the in-laws continued to demand money and beat the victim. The victim had written letters about the harassment. In February 1994 the victim's father was informed that the victim had died in hospital, and he alleged that the in-laws had administered poison. A first information report was lodged the next day against four family members, who were arrested. The prosecution relied on the oral statements of the victim's father and brother and on several letters written by the victim, including one to her father about the in-laws and the gold chain, one to a brother-in-law saying her husband beat her daily, and one about her mother-in-law's dislike of her cooking. A written memorandum dated January 1992, said to record a settlement executed by the in-laws before panchayat members, was also relied upon, though no panchayat member was examined. The death was attributed to organophosphorus pesticide poisoning.

value: On the evening of 1 November 1983, a group of men armed with spears and lathis surrounded the victim and another man who were walking together. Both injured witnesses said they were taken to hospital with the victim, where their injuries were examined. One injured witness showed scars from his injuries while testifying. The officer-in-charge of the police station testified that he requested the injury reports of the witnesses, which were then made available to him before he filed the charge sheet. value: On 25 May 1994 at about 2 pm, the victim was allegedly beaten with lathis by a group of five accused at a place called Brar Khora, near a path between two villages. value: The prosecution case is that the victim had a dispute with one of the accused over the cultivation of a plot of land, which led to an exchange of abuses and threats that the victim would be killed. Later the same day, around noon, the victim sat on a cot in the courtyard of another villager's house while the victim's uncle went to get an agricultural implement repaired. The uncle heard a noise and returned to find six accused standing outside the house, armed with a lathi, two guns, two axes and a pitchfork. One accused allegedly directed that the victim be killed. Two accused fired three shots each from the entrance of the house, two others struck the victim with axes, and another struck with a pitchfork. The victim died on the spot. Other villagers arrived, and the accused threatened them before running away. The uncle dictated a written complaint immediately afterwards. It was scribed by a teacher who reached the spot around 12:45 pm, and was taken to the police station and registered as a first information report. The post-mortem doctor recorded six firearm entry wounds, several incised wounds and firearm exit wounds, and opined that death occurred between 12 and 12:30 pm. The investigation included a site plan and the seizure of guns. The ballistic report was not proved. Two eyewitnesses gave evidence supporting the prosecution account.
