value: A decomposed body was found inside a jute bag in a field beside a bypass road, with maggots around it. The face had been disfigured by acid, so the body was identified only from its clothing by two sons-in-law of the victim. A dupatta was wrapped around the neck with two turns. The postmortem found a fracture of the hyoid bone, an irregular wound over the left chest, and fractures of the sixth and seventh ribs. The chemical examination detected aluminium phosphide insecticide in intestinal samples and phosphine in decomposed organs. A small telephone diary was found in the undershirt pocket of the body. A witness reported seeing a man and a woman on a TVS motorcycle at about 5:30 am on 22 March 2005 carrying a gunny bag; he could not identify either person. The victim had inherited land from a deceased son and leased part of it to the accused for a yearly rent, but the lease money was not paid, and the victim complained of this to a village sarpanch. After the body was identified, police could not trace the accused in the village. Later, a witness stated that one accused had confessed to him in detail, describing a dupatta, a blow with a chair and acid poured on the face. A bottle of acid was recovered from a house on the basis of a disclosure, a folding iron chair was recovered from another house, and a motorcycle was recovered.

value: The victim, a woman married to the accused in June 1994, died in October 1995 from severe burn injuries, about seventeen months after the marriage. The accused, a police constable, lived with her at his posting. Over the marriage the accused was said to drink alcohol heavily, often arriving at the victim's parents' house drunk, and repeatedly demanded money from the victim and her parents, at one stage insisting she bring several thousand rupees from her family. He also beat and ill-treated the victim, including while intoxicated. The victim's father and mother, a brother-in-law and a relative each described these incidents in evidence, saying the victim had complained to them and that her parents had sent money on two occasions. The victim also wrote a letter to her father describing ill-treatment. When the victim's mother and a sister-in-law visited the accused's house, the accused allegedly abused them and beat them with shoes. On the day of the incident, around 8 a.m., only the victim and the accused were in the house. Evidence showed that the victim had been doused with kerosene and set alight in the kitchen, and a bottle of kerosene lay in the room. Broken bangles were found in the room. The post-mortem and forensic reports showed kerosene on the body and burns heavier on the upper body, including a burnt blouse. The accused's explanation was that the victim's nylon sari caught fire accidentally while she was boiling water on the oven. At the hospital the victim told her father that the accused had poured kerosene on her and set her on fire, and she died that evening. The father lodged a complaint the same day. The investigating officer recorded statements, arranged the post-mortem, obtained the forensic report and filed a charge-sheet.

value: Five women living in one house were found dead on 17 December 2012, with some bodies in a courtyard and others in a room. A relative who was alerted by a child living in the house went to the scene and saw blood from the nose and mouth of the victims and marks of injury on their necks. A post-mortem examination found that all five died of asphyxia due to strangulation, and the deaths were homicidal. The investigating officer prepared a site map and seized a glass whisky bottle, a torch, six strands of black hair from one victim's hand, two white buttons, blood-stained soil and a woollen shawl. Fingerprints lifted from the bottle were reported to match one accused. A forensic report found a shirt button and the buttons from the scene to be similar, and a hair report identified only human hair. Following statements made by the accused, a motorcycle, a sum of cash and a silver anklet were recovered, and one accused's shirt was seized. The prosecution alleged that the killings were committed during a robbery. A child witness said that the accused had come to the house the previous night and that, in the early morning, she had found the door locked from outside. She identified the accused as the persons she had seen with the victims. A witness heard of the accused's visit only through a telephone call, and a motorcycle witness gave conflicting descriptions. The gold ornaments and pearl necklace on the victims' bodies were recorded in the site plan.

value: The victim organisation, a food corporation, alleged that a depot in-charge and other staff conspired with a transporter and a contractor to misappropriate urea fertiliser bags during March 1980. A complaint dated December 1981 led to registration of a first information report, which initially referred to 540 bags. Wagons carrying fertiliser were placed at a railway station for unloading, and delivery was signed for in the delivery book on 24 and 25 March 1980. The prosecution alleged that 500 bags were handed over to a representative who signed gate passes for two trucks, each said to carry 250 bags to the depot. The accused responsible for receipt at the depot gate register and the in-charge who maintained the godown registers were said to have entered the arrival of these bags, although the bags were never delivered. The investigation concluded that the entire 1040 bags were misappropriated. Evidence included depositions of the two truck owners, the drivers and a cleaner, who stated that one truck was diverted to a different location and the other was never used for carrying fertiliser. The gate register, arrival tally book, daily receipt register and godown stock register were examined, together with a chart prepared in October 1982 showing delivery of the 500 bags. A government document examiner, an audit assistant manager, a physical verification officer and the investigating officer also testified. Defence evidence came from a retired assistant depot manager.

value: On the night of 10 July 1988, the victim, an army officer, and a colleague visited a hotel on the main road in Ahmednagar. The prosecution alleged that a quarrel broke out at the hotel between the accused and the two visitors, and that chilli powder was thrown into the eyes of the visitors, after which they ran out. The victim was allegedly chased by the accused and assaulted with a gupti, a knife-type weapon, and fell on the road. A beat constable on patrol nearby stated that he saw the accused chase and assault the victim, and that the accused was wearing a black sando banian and a lungi. The constable took the victim by rickshaw to the police station and then to the civil hospital. At the hospital, a Special Executive Magistrate recorded a dying declaration from the victim around midnight, in which the victim described the assailant's clothing. An offence was registered on that basis. The accused was arrested in the early hours of the following day, and blood-stained clothing, a vest and a lungi, was seized from him, along with a gupti recovered on his information. Chemical analysis found the blood group on the clothing matched the victim's blood group. The victim died on 23 July 1988 and the investigation was extended to a homicide offence. The prosecution examined 14 witnesses. Two independent witnesses and the panch witnesses to the seizure did not support the prosecution. The medical evidence was said to be consistent with the eyewitness account.

value: On a day in March 1998 at about 5.30 pm, the victim was riding a motorcycle with two companions when a group of four men stopped it near a lane. One of the men asked the victim to get down to talk. When the victim got down, one attacker struck the victim on the back with a lathi. The victim ran toward a lane to escape. Two other men allegedly caught hold of the victim's arms, and the accused who had the pistol fired at close range at the victim's face, killing the victim instantly. Three eyewitnesses, two of them the victim's companions on the motorcycle and one nearby, described these acts consistently. The defence alleged no eyewitness was present. The post-mortem found a gunshot wound to the left eye and brain, with gunpowder in the eyes, and nine other injuries on the back, arms, chest and head. The doctor opined that the shot was fired from about one foot away. Following a disclosure, a country-made pistol was recovered from a house. Forensic examination found the pistol operative, but the barrel marks on the bullet were insufficient for decisive matching. The FIR was registered at a police station on the same day at 6 pm, and an inquest was conducted at the scene.

value: The accused sought to take the wife of the victim as a third wife, and over time tried to separate the couple through gifts, financial help and interference in their personal lives. On 01.10.2001 the victim and his wife were abducted and released the same day, and a separate complaint was lodged about that abduction. On 26.10.2001 the wife and victim were taken in a vehicle from Tirunelveli, accompanied by several co-accused. At a culvert on the way, co-accused alighted from a following vehicle and took the victim away, and the accused reportedly instructed them to finish him off. The victim's body was found on 31.10.2001 in a forest area near Kodaikanal, decomposed, and was buried as unidentified. The wife said she was under surveillance and could not file a complaint earlier. Investigation included a confession by one accused who led police to the body and a recovery of the body on that basis; recovery of a wallet and gold chain from another accused's house; identification of the body by the wife and family from photographs, clothes, belongings and a scar on the waist; a superimposition test by an expert; post-mortem findings of death by throttling and a broken hyoid bone; handwriting comparison of hotel records; and petrol pump bills showing the vehicle refuelled en route to Kodaikanal. The victim was last seen with the accused.

value: A written complaint by a housing development director in November 2000 led to an FIR alleging a fraud on a housing authority concerning a flat allotted to the victim. The prosecution case was that several housing authority employees, together with property dealers and a special power of attorney holder, acted on a request purportedly made by the allottee to reduce the flat's cost, and that the original fixed deposit receipt and refund application were found removed or misplaced from the file. The FIR further alleged that a refund cheque of Rs.2,22,263 was withdrawn through a savings bank account opened at a bank branch with a forged signature of the allottee. The investigation later alleged that the accused, then a branch manager at that bank, opened a savings account in the allottee's name in connivance with others, in order to encash the cheque dated 7 January 2000. The prosecution relied on a forensic handwriting report dated 30 December 2002 comparing the signature on the account opening form with the accused's specimen signatures. That report stated that a definite opinion could not be given on the remaining items on the materials available. A further report was later sought from a government examiner of questioned documents, which, according to the submissions recorded, expressed an opinion that the signature on the account opening form tallied with the accused's specimen signatures.

value: On the night of 1 July 1987, at about midnight in a village, a group of men confronted two victims over a long-running dispute about a right of way over land. The accused group was said to be armed: one man carried a spear, another an axe, and others sticks. Both victims were stabbed and struck and died at the spot. Two men present, including the complainant, were injured and were examined by a doctor, whose evidence recorded their wounds. The complainant's statement formed the basis of the first information report, lodged at 7 AM the next morning. Post-mortem examination of the two victims recorded stab wounds to the chest, including wounds to the lungs, consistent with the oral evidence that both had received stab wounds. The accused, arrested later in July, also had injuries examined by the same doctor. Their account was that the victims' side, nine in number, had attacked them, and the investigating officer testified that one accused was lying bleeding at the scene. The injured eyewitnesses described the attackers as armed with spears and other weapons. The accused's first account, lodged as a cross-complaint, stated that the victims were not armed.

value: On the intervening night of 31 August and 1 September 2010, the accused is alleged to have strangled the victim, his wife, on the rooftop of a residential premises in Delhi, causing her death. The primary eyewitness was the couple's son, who testified that he saw the accused strangling his mother with an iron rod (saria) after she had taken money from the accused's wallet. The son's account was the central prosecution evidence. A police sub-inspector, the first officer to reach the scene, found the victim's body on the terrace along with a saria, an empty liquor bottle and a plastic glass. A worker in the workshop on the premises testified that he saw the accused leaving the premises in the morning of 1 September 2010. Two further prosecution witnesses confirmed the accused's presence at the scene. The case was registered as an FIR on 1 September 2010 under sections 302 and 34 of the Penal Code. The investigation and trial relied on these eyewitness, last-seen and scene-based evidence, together with the recovered rod.

value: On 16 October 2016, around midday, the victim was with several friends near a medical store when a pillion rider on a motorcycle attacked him with a sharp-edged machete, striking the right side of his neck, and then fled. The victim was declared dead on arrival at hospital. According to the prosecution, the victim was dressed in uniform during a march organised by an association that day, and his throat was cut in a single blow. The case was first registered as a murder by local police, and four persons were arrested within weeks. A fifth person, the accused, was arrested later. The investigation was then taken over by a national investigating agency, which alleged that the accused and four co-accused conspired to kill members of that association. The prosecution relied on call data records showing frequent telephone contact between the accused and co-accused before and after the incident, bank account details, and a seized banner bearing the photographs of all the accused. It also relied on a disclosure leading to a letter listing earlier killings, and on an allegation that the accused had organised indoctrination classes about eight to nine months earlier that the co-accused attended. One co-accused was alleged to have named the accused as the mastermind. The accused denied any personal animosity toward the victim and said nothing incriminating had been recovered from him.

value: The victim left home in the morning, saying he would visit a relative in a nearby village and then report for duty. He did not return by evening, and his mobile phone was switched off. The next morning the victim's daughter was told by a forest guard that he had not reported for duty. She then telephoned a person who lived opposite her house and asked for a contact number at the village. At about 7:15 am on the following day, the police received a telephone call from one of the accused reporting that the victim had died of a gunshot. A police team went towards the place of occurrence. Later that day the victim's daughter gave a statement naming two accused as the shooters, saying she had learned this from police when they came to the village. The police took the two accused, two local witnesses and the daughter to a forest about two kilometres from the house. There the victim's body was found, along with a bag and two pellet marks on nearby bushes. Both accused were said to have made disclosure statements in the presence of the two witnesses, leading to the body and a single-barrel gun with cartridges being recovered; the gun was licensed to a third person and was found at his house. Forensic examination reported that a cartridge had been fired from the gun and that gunshot residue on the victim's clothes indicated distant firing. The post-mortem found multiple perforated gunshot wounds and recorded death from cardio-respiratory failure and hypovolemic shock due to gunshot injury. Both witnesses to the disclosure statements later denied in cross-examination that any such statement was made in their presence. The investigating officer's accounts of when the death became known were said to be contradictory, and no call records were produced to verify the telephone call. The alleged motive was a land dispute with one of the accused.

value: On 22 October 1992 at about 11 a.m., a quarrel broke out between the accused and the victim over the victim's cultivation of land that the accused had been given for cultivation. The two had a pre-existing land dispute, and the victim was related to a co-accused, who was also related to the accused. The accused stopped the victim on his way to the field and told him not to cultivate the land. The argument grew heated with raised voices, and about 50 to 60 villagers gathered. A co-accused, cycling past, stopped and intervened. The victim told him not to interfere and to go home. The co-accused took a country-made pistol from his trouser pocket, pointed it at the victim, and fired. The victim was struck by splinters on the forehead near his eye, on his lips and on his shoulder, and bled. The victim testified that the accused urged the co-accused to kill him; an eyewitness testified that the accused told the co-accused to beat the victim. A medical officer said the injuries were caused by firearm splinters. After the firing the co-accused fled and the accused followed him. The victim lodged a report at a police chowki, a case was registered, and the investigating officer examined the victim and eyewitnesses and seized blood-stained clothing. Several witnesses did not support the prosecution.

value: A dispute existed between two family groups over use of an unrecorded passage that ran through fields owned by some of the accused and that the victim's group used to reach its own land. Earlier, a similar obstruction had been settled through local intervention. On the day of the incident, a quarrel broke out between a member of the victim's group and one of the accused over the passage, and the parties dispersed. At sunset, the complainant, a member of the victim's group, was walking alone towards the village when several men came out from behind a thicket of bushes near a pond and surrounded him. Some carried sharp-edged weapons and others carried sticks. One of the men allegedly swung a sharp-edged weapon at the complainant, who raised his hand and was wounded on the palm. Other members of the victim's group then arrived from their fields. One of them caught hold of the weapon, and the victim allegedly was struck on the head from behind with a sharp-edged weapon by one of the accused and fell. Beatings from both sides followed until other villagers intervened, after which the assailants ran away. The victim died of the head wound. Prosecution evidence included eyewitness depositions of several persons from the victim's group, the post-mortem report describing a deep incised wound to the head with the underlying bone and brain membranes cut, injury reports for both sides, the first information report lodged that night, a spot inspection memo and site plan, and recovery of a blood-stained lathi and blood-stained clothing of the injured and deceased.

value: On 10 July 1999, the victim, an advocate, was sitting in his residential office dictating to his stenographer, with his clerk present. At about 5:30 pm, the accused, a police constable, entered the office in an inebriated condition, claiming to be a beat officer, and asked for water. After drinking the water, the accused pulled out his service pistol, pointed it at the victim and said he would kill ten people that day. The accused asked the victim to stand with raised hands and directed the clerk and stenographer to leave the room. The accused then moved around the table towards the victim and pulled the lever to ready the weapon. The victim lunged and pushed the accused's hand upward, and a bullet struck the ceiling. No one was injured. The accused tried to fire again, but a bullet fell from the pistol. Household members entered and raised an alarm, and the accused fled, leaving a wireless set behind. Police arrived within about 10 to 15 minutes and arrested the accused nearby with the pistol still in hand. A medical examination recorded that the accused was under the influence of alcohol; the accused declined to give urine or blood samples. A forensic report found that the cartridge recovered from the office was fired from the accused's pistol. The stenographer testified that he saw the shot fired through a mesh door, and the clerk testified to the accused's drunken state and to hearing the shot. The victim testified to the sequence of events.

value: On the evening of 23 January 2014, around 8.30 pm, six members of one family were attacked and killed with knives at their house in a village. According to the prosecution, the victims were killed in the courtyard, the verandah, rooms in the middle portion of the house and an upstairs room. Blood-stained clothes were later recovered from another house. Forensic science reports were obtained. A fingerprint expert report and a dog squad report were not placed on record, and no independent villager witness was examined.

value: On a night in February, the complainant's family had returned home from a wedding function in a nearby village with food. At about 8 pm, while the family was eating, a group of villagers came to the house, shouted for the complainant and his father to come out, and began pelting stones. The family retreated and bolted the door, but the group broke it open and entered the house armed with axes, sickles, spears and sticks. It is alleged that one accused struck an elderly relative of the complainant on the head with an axe, causing death on the spot, and that another accused struck the complainant's father with an axe, causing him to faint. Other assailants beat the complainant with sticks, and he escaped to the roof. Some bystanders intervened and the attackers left. The complainant walked through the night to the police station and lodged a First Information Report the next morning. Police recovered sticks, a blood-stained stone, glass splinters, pieces of wood, broken door pieces, a broken bulb and blood-stained soil from the house, and an axe from one accused. Blood marks were also found on a path outside the house. The post-mortem found one fatal sharp-edged head injury, which the doctor said could have been caused by the recovered axe. The injured man had incised wounds on the face and back of the skull and a facial bone fracture, which the doctor said could be caused by an axe. The complainant, his wife and his father gave consistent eyewitness accounts of the attack.

value: On the intervening night of 2 and 3 August 2006, at about 2.30 to 3.00 am, a fire broke out in a small house of three rooms. The house was occupied by the accused, the accused's husband, the husband's first wife, the first wife's two children, the husband's parents and a servant who occupied one room. The husband had gone to another town that day to buy tractor tyres, and the mother-in-law had gone to her daughter's home. The accused came out of the house without any injury. The first wife and her daughter ran out with burn injuries, while the son died inside the house. The father-in-law, who had been sleeping on a cot outside, woke in the confusion and arranged for a jeep to take the injured to hospital. The first wife and daughter died the next day from their burns. Police seized the daughter's burnt frock from the scene under a panchnama and sent it for chemical analysis, which reported kerosene residues. A kerosene can said to smell of kerosene was recovered from nearby bushes at the accused's instance, but it was not sent for chemical analysis. The father-in-law stated that the accused had made an extra-judicial confession to him that kerosene had been sprinkled and the fire set. A sister of the first wife gave evidence of an oral dying declaration, and a police head constable recorded a separate dying declaration. The first wife's declaration said the household slept in the house with a lantern lit at night, and that cooking and tractor diesel were kept there. Medical evidence was presented on the cause of the deaths.

value: The victim, a 12-year-old girl, is the niece of the accused, who is her maternal uncle. It is alleged that on 14 December 2021, at the accused's house where the victim and her mother had stayed for some days, the accused asked the victim to sit on his lap. He then hugged her, kissed her on the cheeks and tried to kiss her on the lips. It is alleged that he attempted to remove her top, touched her breasts and made sexual comments, and that the victim cried out, after which he released her. The allegations state that the incident occurred in an upstairs bedroom while no other person was present. The victim, previously an excellent student, afterwards declined markedly in her studies, with her grades falling from mostly A grades in sixth standard to mostly C grades in seventh standard. She was taken for counselling. In the first session she did not open up, and in the second session she disclosed the incident. She had not told her mother earlier, out of fear. The complaint was made about six months after the incident. A first information report was registered on 27 May 2022. A medical examination of the victim was conducted, and her statement under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was recorded. Her statements to the police and to a magistrate describe the incident. The counsellor's statement and the victim's school report form part of the material.

value: The victim was travelling on the rear seat of a scooty driven by her servant, returning from a district court in the evening. Near a temple, the victim and her driver saw a car with several persons parked nearby. The car followed the scooty and, near a village, rammed into it, and both the victim and the driver fell onto the road. The car then stopped near the driver, and a person in it shouted that the driver should also be killed because he might give evidence. The assailants fled when passers-by gathered. Passers-by helped the driver take the victim to a hospital, where she died. An autopsy was conducted that night. The victim's sister lodged a written report the next day, alleging prior enmity between the family and the accused. Investigation later relied on call recordings between co-accused, provided to the investigating officer by the complainant, which led to the identification of additional accused. Investigators found that the daughters of the victim's late father had been in prolonged litigation over the division of his immovable properties. The prosecution's case was that one accused was the leader of an organised gang who planned the killing for pecuniary gain, with other co-accused, including the later-added accused, joining in. A gang chart was prepared and a supplementary charge sheet was filed against the later-added accused.

value: On an evening in January 2007, at about 8:30 p.m., a group of eleven accused persons, armed with hunting sickles, allegedly emerged from behind a sumo vehicle and surrounded it near a clinic in Kurnool. The vehicle was carrying the victim, the victim's brother, other occupants and a driver. Three of the accused allegedly forcibly opened the front left door, dragged the victim out, and hacked him repeatedly with hunting sickles, causing his death on the spot. Other accused allegedly struck the vehicle's glass windows with sickles and broke them. Two accused allegedly hacked the driver, causing bleeding injuries to his shoulder, hand and ribs. Further accused allegedly chased the fleeing occupants, and one occupant was injured. The injured driver and another injured occupant were taken to hospital. A first information report was lodged on the statement of the victim's brother, and the investigating officer recorded witness statements, collected medical and documentary evidence, and arrested the accused. The prosecution relied on the testimony of three eyewitnesses, two injured eyewitnesses and the medical evidence. The accused denied the charges.

value: At about 12:45 a.m. on 21 April 2011, the victim was shot dead on a street in Jalandhar. The prosecution case was that the victim believed a raid on a hotel run by his family had been instigated by the accused, and that a quarrel preceded the incident. A witness who went looking for the victim saw the accused grappling with him under a street light. A friend of the victim was also present; this witness later turned hostile at trial. The prosecution alleged that, shortly before the shooting, two of the accused made the remark 'what are you seeing now', after which another accused, who had already drawn a gun and brandished it at the victim, took out a gun from his pocket and fired a single shot. The victim was taken to a hospital about three kilometres away in a car, and a complaint was lodged. The investigating officer completed the investigation and recovered weapons. Medical evidence was on record. A further witness claimed to have overheard a prior plan to commit the murder, but this account was contested. The defence examined its own witnesses. The evidence on the fight and the sequence of events was disputed in its details, including the supplementary statement attributed to the victim's father.

value: The incident arose from a dispute over a boundary wall on land claimed by the victim. The victim was repairing a mud wall that had fallen in rain, with the help of hired labourers. A neighbour objected to the repair work and said the land was his. A verbal altercation followed. The neighbour went to his house and returned with a second man, both carrying guns. Two other men then arrived carrying a spear and a lathi. The two armed men fired shots at the victim. One shot struck the victim's left leg and another struck the victim's right arm or hand. The other two men then assaulted the victim with a spear and a lathi. On hearing the gunshots, family members and villagers came to the scene, and the four men ran away. The victim was taken to a private clinic. The doctor who examined the victim recorded entry and exit wounds on the right forearm and left leg, with charring of the skin at one site. He stated that all injuries were caused by firearms and were simple in nature. He also stated that tattooing may not appear over a wound if fired from 6-7 feet. Several eyewitnesses, including family members and persons present nearby, testified that the two armed men were present, carried guns and fired at the victim after the altercation. Some witnesses were declared hostile. One of the accused said he was posted elsewhere on duty that day, and a defence witness supported this, but a prosecution witness said he was present at the scene. The investigating officer recorded the victim's statement, visited the scene and noted an ongoing dispute over the land.

value: On the day before the incident, the accused quarrelled with the victim, who was the accused's uncle, and abused him; the victim sharply reprimanded the accused. The next morning, at about 10:30 to 11:00 a.m., the victim was walking towards the village bus stand when the accused approached from the opposite direction carrying a wooden side of a cot frame. The accused abused the victim for shouting at and insulting him the previous day, said he would teach him a lesson, and struck the victim once on the head. The victim fell down, and the accused ran away with the wooden piece. Two of the victim's sons, who were standing outside a nearby shop, took their bleeding father to Civil Hospital, Giddarbaha, from where he was referred to Dayanand Medical College, Ludhiana. The victim died the following day. The complainant son gave a written statement to a police officer, which was endorsed and sent for registration of an FIR. Police visited the spot, prepared a rough site plan and lifted blood-stained earth. At the hospital, an inquest was prepared, and a post-mortem found eight injuries, the main one on the head; the doctor opined the cause of death was shock and haemorrhage from the head injury. The accused was arrested some weeks later and, in police presence, indicated where the blood-stained wooden piece was concealed in a wheat chaff room at the accused's residence; it was recovered. Chemical examination found the blood on the piece and on the spot earth matched the victim. Two eyewitnesses, the victim's sons, testified that the accused struck the victim's head with the wooden piece.

value: On the night of 2–3 November 2015, at about 3 a.m., the victim and his wife woke up. While the wife was preparing to cook, the victim went out to attend to the call of nature. The wife heard the victim shouting that four persons were attacking him. She ran to the spot and saw two of the accused assaulting the victim with an axe, while two other accused were holding him. On her raising a loud alarm, all of them ran away. She found the victim bleeding. He told her that four of them had caught hold of him and attacked him with an axe. She gave him water at his request, and neighbours carried him into the house. He was then taken to a hospital by auto, where he was declared dead. The reason for the assault was alleged to be an evil eye kept by the victim on the wife of one of the accused. The wife's statements were recorded under Section 161 and later Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. A first information report was registered on 3 November 2015 and, after investigation, a charge sheet was filed. Four persons were charged with murder read with common intention. The wife, as the only eyewitness, gave evidence of the incident as described. No dying declaration was recorded, as the victim was declared dead on arrival at the hospital.

value: The accused was charged with raping and murdering a six-year-old girl, who was a relative of the accused. According to the complaint lodged by the victim's uncle, at about 4:00 p.m. on 8 March 2012, during the Holi festival, the accused took the victim away on the pretext of showing dance and song performances. When the victim did not return home, a search was made. The accused was not found at home, and the victim's body was found in a sugarcane field on the southern side of the village. A member of the search party stated that he saw the accused leaving the sugarcane field about half an hour later. Another villager said he saw the accused carrying the victim towards the sugarcane field. The prosecution case rested on these eyewitness accounts and on the last-seen circumstance. The FIR was registered at the police station on the evening of 8 March 2012. The post-mortem was conducted by a doctor, who prepared a vaginal smear. A salwar bearing stains was sent for forensic examination, but no forensic report was obtained. The accused was not subjected to medical examination. The investigating officer recorded witness statements and prepared a site map. The victim's clothing, including a salwar, was recovered by the police.

value: On the night of 24 June 1987, the victim was travelling on a scooter with two companions on a separate scooter toward a village to attend a marriage. Near a road turn at about 9.30 pm, the two companions say that in the scooter light they saw three uniformed men on the road, one carrying a stick and two carrying rifles. The man with the stick flashed a torch at them, and the two scooters skidded. One of the uniformed men allegedly urged others to shoot, and shots were fired. The victim was hit, collapsed, and was taken to a hospital in the presence of police, but died on the way. The two companions escaped to the village. The FIR was lodged by one companion, and a separate case was registered on a rival version describing an armed criminal group and police retaliatory fire, in which two empty cartridge shells were recovered from the spot. Villagers and police arrived at the scene. Three uniformed constables were on patrol that night and had left the police station with rifles and 50 rounds each. Ballistic examination found that some empty cartridges at the spot were fired from the service rifles of two of the constables, while two others were not matched to any of the three. The autopsy showed the fatal injury came from a .12 bore gun, which was not recovered from any of the accused. One witness claimed to have seen the accused fire a country-made pistol, and the accused were said to have remained at the spot after the incident.

value: The victim, a police constable working as record keeper at a police station, was using the station's official telephone in the reporting room for five to seven minutes. The duty officer, a sub-inspector, told the victim to free the line because urgent calls might come in, but the victim continued the call. Around 5.55 pm the duty officer asked the accused, a guard posted at the station and carrying a semi-automatic fire carbine, to ask the victim to end the call. The accused entered the room, placed a hand on the victim's shoulder and asked the victim to end the call. The prosecution's initial account was that the victim playfully pushed the accused while holding the carbine. During the struggle the carbine became entangled in the chain attached to the accused's belt, and five rounds fired. Five bullets struck the victim in the neck and chest. The victim was taken to hospital and declared dead. An offence was first registered on the duty officer's statement. The victim's father complained to senior police officers, and the investigation was transferred to the Crime Branch, which alleged that the victim had seen the accused and the duty officer in a compromising position and that they had threatened to kill him. Ballistic reports recorded close-range firing. A later report stated that the carbine could be cocked by entanglement with a chain if the change lever was not at the safety position, and would then fire if the trigger was pressed. Eyewitness accounts described the entanglement and accidental firing. A witness said he heard the accused tell the duty officer that the accused's children would be ruined, and heard the duty officer's reply. Several other persons present did not support the prosecution.

value: In the late evening of the incident, the victim was allegedly assaulted with lathis in an open street in front of a house in a village, by several men identified as the accused. Two eyewitnesses said they saw the assault. One of them had earlier given a police statement that differed from his court testimony, and the other was not present when the assault began and said he came out after an alarm that the victim was beating the son of one of the accused. Neither eyewitness lodged a report. A named first information report was lodged the next morning at about 10 am by a village chowkidar of a neighbouring village, who said no eyewitness had informed her; she had come to the spot after hearing loud noises and found the body near a temple. Villagers guarded the body overnight. The next day, the police conducted an inquest, collected blood-stained earth from the spot, and seized a lathi lying near the body. The site plan showed that the body was about 300 feet from the place of assault, and drag marks were noticed. value: The victim was married to the accused in 1987 and the couple had two children. The victim's family alleged that the accused harassed the victim because of insufficient dowry. The admitting doctor recorded that the victim said her husband had poured water to extinguish the fire. On 7 November the victim regained consciousness and told relatives the accused had set her on fire. The victim's relatives applied to a sub-divisional magistrate, and an Executive Magistrate recorded the victim's statement on 8 November after a doctor's fitness opinion. The statement attributed the burning to the accused and two in-laws, who had held the victim while kerosene was poured. An FIR was registered on that statement. The investigating officer concluded the case was not one of attempted murder or cruelty and found the victim was short-tempered. The victim later died, and a death report was sent to police on 18 November 1991.

value: On the morning of 17 April 1988, the victim was being taken by his son to a hospital for treatment, with a companion riding pillion. Upon reaching a particular house, eleven persons attacked them with country-made bombs, lathis and tabbal (shovels). The victim received multiple injuries and died during treatment. The companion ran off and hid in a nearby house for about two hours, suffering numerous injuries, including lacerated wounds and serious damage to his left eye. The victim's son was found alive near a tree close to the scene. He was taken to a government hospital and then to a private hospital, where he died the same day. The police reached the scene at about 11.15 a.m. after a report recorded at 11.00 a.m. at the companion's instance. The FIR recorded the incident time as 8.15 a.m. Three eyewitnesses, including the companion, the victim's wife and a relative of the victim, testified that the accused were present at the scene and attacked the victim with bombs, lathis and shovels. The investigating sub-inspector found the complicity of all eleven persons and filed a challan.

value: On the morning of 14 May 2004, at about 6:00 a.m., the accused attacked the victim with an iron locking plate inside a store where the victim was working. The store belonged to the brother of the accused's grandfather. The prosecution alleged there was no motive, no provocation and no premeditation. An eyewitness saw the incident. After the assault, the accused took the object out of the store, walked to a nearby bus stand, returned and left the object in the shop, then went back to the bus stand and sat on a chair without attempting to leave. Before the incident, the accused had been an in-patient at a government hospital in Bhiwani, Haryana, from 17 to 26 November 2003. The records noted anxiety neurosis with reactive depression, symptoms of acid peptic disease and mild hypertension. The treatment given was akin to that for schizophrenia, and the medicine Thioril was prescribed. After the incident, a government doctor examined the accused. She later certified that the accused had chronic schizophrenia, probably from around age 14 or 15, and was not fit to stand trial. A later certificate, issued after in-patient treatment, stated the accused could stand trial. Her statement was recorded about sixteen years after the occurrence. An uncle of the accused testified about the earlier treatment. A relative of the accused's grandfather who was examined found no abnormality. The doctor who physically examined the accused after the incident stated the accused was mentally well.

value: Following secret information, police conducted a raid on 28 September 2015 and allegedly found about 180 kilograms of ganja in the possession of four persons, who were arrested. During the investigation, one of the arrested persons was taken to another state to identify co-accused persons. At his instance, the accused was arrested in the early hours of 3-4 October 2015. The accused was not found in possession of any narcotic drug, and no other contraband was recovered from him. The prosecution alleged that another co-accused purchased ganja and transferred money from his bank account to the bank accounts of the accused and others before supplying the drug to a further person. Bank statements of that co-accused were relied upon to show that money had been transferred to the accused. Call records were said to show regular contact between the accused and the co-accused. The prosecution also relied on a confessional statement given by the accused. The prosecution alleged that the accused was the mastermind behind the supply of narcotic substances from another state, but no evidence of extensive dealing in narcotics was identified, and no involvement in other cases was shown. Two co-accused persons, who were not present at the raid and from whom no contraband was recovered, were the recipients of the transfers and the holders of documents relating to a seized car. One witness reportedly stated during trial that Rs. 50,000 was received from the accused. A chargesheet was filed on 29 February 2016.

value: On the night of 21 August 2008, two accused entered a house while the victim's father, who also ran a gold and silver business from the premises, was away. The accused concealed iron rods under their clothing and attacked two inmates, the victim's son and the victim's wife, who were both killed. Gold ornaments of about 3.5 kg and cash of Rs 18,340 were taken. The father returned to the house around 10 pm to 10:30 pm, after receiving word of loud cries from the house, and found the bodies in pools of blood near iron rods, with gold missing from the shop almirah and showcase. Neighbours had gathered outside. Three witnesses, independent of one another and with no known animosity toward the accused, each said they saw one or both accused running away from the house that night carrying bags. Medical officers recorded death from brain injury and haemorrhage following a head injury and found the deaths homicidal; blood-stained iron rods were found near the bodies. Following a written report lodged around 11 pm, police apprehended one accused at about 1.15 am carrying a bag containing gold ornaments and cash, and that accused allegedly confessed. The second accused was arrested at about 4 am and produced a bag with gold ornaments; blood-stained clothing was seized from both. The father identified the ornaments at an identification parade conducted with independent witnesses. Chance fingerprints lifted from the shop showcase and a plastic box were compared with the accused's specimen prints.

value: Late on the night of the incident, the victim was talking with a friend near a car consultancy shop in a slum area when one of the accused passing by approached him, and a verbal exchange followed. Shortly afterwards, the accused arrived with others and a fight broke out. The victim's friend was struck on the head with a sickle and a sword and was bleeding. The victim was then severely attacked with a sickle and a sword, receiving multiple wounds to the hands, wrist, arm, shoulder and chest. A neighbour came out of his house during the assault and asked what the fighting was about. The injured friend asked a rickshaw driver known to them to watch the victim and then went with a neighbour to the police station to report the incident. Police took the victim to hospital, where he was declared dead. The post-mortem examination found multiple injuries, including a stab wound to the right chest that cut the ribs and entered the lung. The doctor opined that this injury was sufficient in the ordinary course to cause death, and that the injuries were caused by sharp-edged weapons. Three eyewitnesses gave oral evidence, including the injured friend, the neighbour and the rickshaw driver. The rickshaw driver stated that the injured friend told him what had happened. Following statements made by the accused in police custody, weapons were recovered in the presence of panch witnesses. A chargesheet was filed after investigation.

value: The accused married the victim in October 1992, and a male child was born to them in December 1993. Earlier, the victim had lodged a first information report alleging cruelty by the accused and had filed a complaint under Sections 107/151 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and a petition seeking maintenance for herself and her child. The victim later returned to the matrimonial home. On 26 September 1994, at about 1:45 a.m., the victim consumed tablets of aluminium phosphide, an insecticide. She was taken to hospital but died at about 5:00 a.m. the same day. The police recorded the death in the daily diary register and sent the body for post-mortem. On 1 October 1994 the victim's brother lodged a first information report alleging that the accused had subjected the victim to cruelty and forced her to commit suicide. After investigation, a chargesheet was filed under Sections 498-A and 306 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution relied on the victim's three earlier proceedings against the accused, the fact of poisoning and death, and the fact that the death occurred within seven years of marriage. The accused was said to have told investigators that the victim took the tablets by mistake, believing them to be insecticide, and had not informed the victim's parents immediately after the incident. The defence relied on a suicide note stating the victim acted because of intolerable pain and illness, and on two neighbours who said the couple's relationship was cordial.

value: On an evening at about 9.45 pm, the victim was sitting in the courtyard of the home with the victim's wife, talking. Four men from the same village came to the courtyard. The prosecution alleged that they said they would teach the victim a lesson for refusing to give them jaggery (gur), and that one of them fired a firearm at the victim. The shot struck the victim's right chest and arm. The victim's son and grandson, who were nearby, heard the shot, reached the courtyard within moments and reported seeing the four men fleeing. The victim was taken to a government hospital, where a doctor declared the victim dead. A written report was lodged the following day and a case was registered. The investigating officer inspected the scene, prepared an inquest report and a site plan, and seized a torch, a lantern, bloodstained soil, a bloodstained cot and bedding. Acting on information given by one accused, police recovered a 12-bore country-made pistol and one empty cartridge from a field near a transformer. The post-mortem found two firearm wounds of entry, on the right arm and right chest, with blackening and tattooing around them; death was due to shock and haemorrhage from firearm injuries, and both wounds could have been caused by one bullet. Eyewitnesses testified that the accused were armed and that one of them fired on the exhortation of the others. One eyewitness explained the source of light at the scene. The investigating officer's account differed on whether the shooting was instigated by others. Several discrepancies in the prosecution evidence were noted.

value: The body of the victim was found in a paddy field in the early morning of 17 August 1989 by a passer-by on his way to work. A postmortem examination found six antemortem injuries on the left side of the head, fractured into multiple fragments, plus abraded contusions on the right wrist and left knee. The head injuries were sufficient to cause death and could have been caused by a coconut scraper. The medical expert estimated death about 30 to 35 hours before the postmortem. The prosecution alleged that the accused and a co-accused were in an illicit relationship, and that the victim often stayed at the co-accused's house. The victim's mother and sister said the victim left for that house around 7:30 PM on 16 August. The co-accused's two children said the victim left their house around 9:00 PM and did not return. A witness said he saw the back of a person he assumed was the accused entering the house around 11:30 PM. The prosecution alleged that during an altercation about the relationship, the accused struck the victim on the head repeatedly with a coconut scraper, dragged the body out, and carried it about one kilometre to the paddy field. A taxi driver said he saw a man he identified as the accused at a bus stand at about 5:30 AM on 17 August, wearing a shirt, lungi and towel. A bag said to contain blood-stained clothes, a blanket and a head towel belonging to the accused was said to have been recovered on 27 August. Blood-stained cotton swabs, cloth and the coconut scraper were said to have been recovered from the co-accused's house, in the presence of three witnesses who said they were only shown the items.

value: The victim had been married to the accused for about twelve years and lived in the matrimonial home with the victim's in-laws. No child was born in the first five years of the marriage, and the victim was allegedly subjected to physical and mental harassment on that account, leading to a return to the parental home for a time. After the victim returned to the matrimonial home, a son was born. About twelve months before the death, the victim told the victim's father that the accused had sold gold ornaments the victim had received as streedhan at the marriage. When the victim demanded their return, the victim was allegedly physically and mentally harassed. On 18 April 2021 the victim's father was informed that the victim had died by hanging. It was alleged that the harassment by the accused compelled the victim to take the victim's own life. An FIR was registered on the same day at the victim's father's instance. The investigation produced the FIR, the investigating officer's chargesheet findings, and statements of the victim's father, other witnesses and the victim's cousins. These described repeated complaints by the victim of physical and mental harassment by the accused, including the sale of the ornaments and harassment on demand for their return. The cousins' statements mentioned only incidents that occurred about a year before the death.

value: On the evening of 10 April 2004 the victim left a workplace on his motorcycle after receiving two phone calls, saying he had to go to a market. The next morning his family reported him missing. His body was later found lying in a field with his throat tied with cloth, one eye badly injured and injuries to the head. The post-mortem doctor found an incised wound that, in the doctor's view, was caused by a sharp-edged weapon. Investigators recorded statements from several persons. One witness said he saw four young men on a motorcycle carrying sticks near a bypass that evening, one of them with blood-stained clothing, and noted a registration number. Another said he saw three young men on a motorcycle holding sticks at a road junction around 10 pm and recognised one of them. A third said he saw the victim seated on a motorcycle with one of the accused at a junction. After a surrender, the accused were said to have made an extra-judicial confession before a village sarpanch, who also said he had seen the victim earlier that evening. Police recovered sticks, a pair of trousers and a mobile phone. Forensic tests reported blood of the same group as the victim on the sticks and trousers. No sharp-edged weapon was recovered. The recoveries were not made in the presence of any independent witness. The case rested entirely on circumstantial evidence, with no eyewitness to the killing.

value: On an evening in January 1999, the victim's brother (the informant) and the informant's son were sitting together warming themselves by a fire when the victim was about to walk home. Three men came to the spot to confront the victim over a fight that had broken out between them the previous day. One man carried a pharsa, another a kulhari and the third a lathi. According to the informant's first information report, one attacker struck the victim on the head with a pharsa and another struck him with the same weapon. A third blow was struck with a kulhari. When the victim fell, the lathi-carrying man struck his legs, and a further pharsa blow was delivered to his head. A person who tried to rescue the victim was struck on the shoulder with a lathi. The victim died about two days later from his injuries. A medical examination recorded four incised wounds to the scalp, and the rescuer had two blunt injuries. Police arrested the accused in stages. A lathi was recovered from one accused and a kulhari from another, and a blood-stained pharsa was recovered from a third. The fourth named person had no recovery made against him. The informant and the injured rescuer gave eyewitness accounts of the attack.

value: The victim and the first accused married in 2007, and a male child was born in 2008. Around January 2009, a passport application for the minor child was submitted to the Regional Passport Office, Bengaluru, and a passport was issued shortly afterwards. The accused side contends that the victim had consented to the passport and later sent a sponsorship letter citing the child's passport number. The victim lodged a complaint on 13 May 2010, registered as an FIR under sections 420, 468 and 471 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The first accused had earlier complained of cruelty by the victim and his family. During the investigation, the charges under sections 468 and 471 were initially dropped. The State Forensic Laboratory expressed no opinion on the questioned photocopied signatures, citing bad line quality of strokes. A private laboratory report obtained by the victim, dated 15 July 2013, opined that the signatures did not closely resemble the victim's specimen signatures. A passport officer was implicated for allegedly withholding the original passport application. A supplementary chargesheet was later filed.

value: The victim was travelling to a nearby town in an auto-rickshaw on a morning in November 2001, with two co-passengers. The accused are four men from the same village and family group as the victim. Earlier, a relative of the victim had won a village council election against the wife of one accused, and the resulting rivalry between the two groups is alleged to be the motive. When the auto-rickshaw reached a house belonging to one accused, one accused stopped the vehicle and pulled the victim out by his legs. Another accused joined in and dragged him toward that house. The accused are alleged to have attacked him with an axe, a sword, a stone and a knife. The victim's son, an eyewitness, reported the matter to the police the same evening. The investigating officer found the body in the front yard of the house, took photographs, prepared a sketch, and conducted an inquest in the presence of panch witnesses. The post-mortem recorded twelve injuries, ten caused by sharp-edged weapons, including a partial amputation of three fingers of the left hand and a deep lacerated wound at the back of the neck. The cause of death was given as cardio-pulmonary arrest due to transection of the spinal cord at the atlanto-occipital joint. On 23 November 2001 the accused were apprehended. One accused gave a confessional statement, after which an axe, a sword and a knife were recovered from bushes in a field. Several eyewitnesses described the sequence of the assault, the weapons used and the role of each accused. Among them, several said one accused struck the victim's head with a stone. Recovered objects were sent for forensic examination.

value: On an evening, the victim was sitting on a cot in the open space in front of the family house near the entrance. Her two sons were sitting nearby, and two neighbours sat on another cot. They were chatting under a lantern hanging from the roof. At about 8 pm, the accused arrived from the north with a co-accused. The prosecution alleged that the co-accused told the accused that one son was causing trouble and should be killed. The accused then fired a country-made pistol. The bullet struck the victim's left breast, and she died immediately. The targeted son said he bent below the cot. The witnesses gave differing accounts of where people were sitting and whether the son had stood up. The son lodged a written report at a police station at midnight on the same day, stating that the two men ran away towards the north. The police seized a cartridge tikli from the wound, a 12 bore cartridge from the cot, and 12 pellets from the wound. The post-mortem recovered 55 pellets from the body. The pistol was never recovered. The pellets and tikli were not sent for ballistic examination. Blood-stained clothes and soil samples were sent to a chemical examiner, but no report was received. Another son who was present and the scribe of the report were not examined. A village head said he heard the firing and learned of the death later from a passer-by, who was also not examined. value: On the evening of the incident, the victim and the accused were walking a few steps ahead of the victim's sister-in-law, who was returning from a local market. She saw them grapple with each other and then saw the accused stab the victim several times with a knife the accused was carrying. The victim collapsed and the accused ran away. The victim was first taken to a nearby private clinic and then advised to go to a hospital, where the victim was declared dead on arrival. A post-mortem the next day recorded multiple incised stab wounds on the body. One wound entered the left chest cavity, injuring the pericardium and the tip of the left ventricle; the examining doctor opined that this injury was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, which was due to shock and haemorrhage. The doctor stated that the injuries were possible with the recovered knife, which had been produced in a sealed parcel. An FIR was registered the same day based on the eyewitness's statement. Shortly afterwards, police received information and found the accused coming from the side of a drain, carrying a blood-stained knife and wearing a blood-stained shirt. The accused was apprehended and the knife and shirt were recovered. Forensic analysis found that the victim's blood matched blood on the knife. The eyewitness described the sequence of events in detail, having watched from a short distance, and was cross-examined at length without any material discrediting her testimony.

value: The victim's father owned agricultural land and a house in a village. In the morning of a September day in 2001, the victim went with four farm workers to build a check dam on the family land. The father packed their lunch at midday and visited the field. Work stopped at about 3.30 pm, and the group set off for the village. Near a particular landholding at about 4 pm, several accused allegedly appeared and said that the victim's side had killed a member of their family and that they would take revenge in the same manner. The accused were said to be armed with a jambiya, axes and sickles, and the victim was beaten and fell. The father alleged that he was threatened and hid in bushes until after sunset. He then returned home and told family members. A written complaint was lodged at the police station early the next morning, and an FIR was registered. Investigation led to a charge sheet against the accused and others. Twenty-seven witnesses were examined. Four workers and the father were presented as eyewitnesses, along with another witness. The medical jurist described decomposition of the body and an estimated time of death more than 24 hours before autopsy. Witnesses said it had rained heavily for about three days before the incident. The investigating officer described recoveries of axes, a koyta, a jambiya and sickles made on the basis of statements of the accused. The complainant said police showed him the weapons on the day of the incident. No serological opinion on the weapons was obtained.

value: The victim was a long-serving cash collector and clerk employed by the accused, who ran a wood business. On 15 July 1993 the victim and a companion were collecting business proceeds from shops. While the victim was inside a shop, two men snatched a bag holding the collection from the companion at gunpoint and fled on a motorcycle. The accused reported this as a robbery to the police. The initial investigation found the report to be false, but the case was later reassigned to another officer. On 17 July 1993 the accused had the victim brought from his home through an employee to the police station for inquiry. According to the later investigation report, the victim was then held at the police station until 23 July 1993 and was tortured during interrogation about the robbery. Late on 23 July he was taken to a hospital by police personnel and was admitted under an unknown name. He died in the early hours of 24 July 1993. A complaint by the accused alleged that police personnel had beaten the victim to death. The post mortem report recorded ante mortem cut incisions on both buttocks. The cause of death could not be ascertained and poisoning was ruled out. Section 161 statements of the victim's widow, son and brother were recorded. Under the investigation report, no police station entry of the custody was made.

value: On a day in early April, the victim, a minor boy, went out in his car to play badminton and did not return home that evening. Later that night, his family began receiving telephone calls from unknown callers claiming the boy was in their custody and demanding a ransom of one crore rupees, with threats to kill the boy and harm the family if the police were informed. The family gathered cash from various sources and, on instructions from the callers, left the money in a car at a hospital area and then went to another location. Shortly afterwards the boy was found standing in a market area and was brought home. According to the victim, three men had stopped his car on the way home from the playground, one holding a pistol. He was robbed of his watch, ATM card, identity card, gold chain and cash, blindfolded, and kept confined overnight in a room, where he heard the men calling each other by name. The family did not report the matter to police for about two weeks. Police acted on source information about a kidnapping gang and registered a case without a complaint from the family. The investigating officer traced two mobile numbers used for the ransom calls through the service provider and SIM sale records. Several men were arrested and disclosure statements were recorded, followed by alleged recoveries of cash, a motorcycle, watches, mobile phones, a car and an air pistol. The victim later identified the accused at a later stage of the proceedings, and call detail records were produced.

value: The victim, who had been arraigned as an accused in a criminal case registered at a police station, came to that police station late at night, accompanied by his advocate and two sisters, to surrender. The prosecution case is that two police officers, the accused, assaulted the victim with fists and sticks at separate intervals inside the police station, causing multiple injuries across his body, after which he became unconscious and was placed in a lockup. He was taken to a civil hospital and declared dead early the following morning. Two sisters testified that they saw the beatings, and a third detainee in the lockup also gave evidence. The sisters described blows landing on the back, arms, chest, thighs and ankles. A telegram sent by one sister to the state police headquarters alleged custodial torture, and a formal complaint followed about three weeks after the incident. The post-mortem examination recorded multiple external abrasions and bruises and internal injuries, including fractures of the sternum and ribs and ruptures of the lung, liver and spleen. The medical jurist opined that the injuries were fresh, occurring within six to eight hours of death, and that a person with such injuries could not climb stairs without support. An inquest witness described red dust on the clothing, and the jail soil was said to be red. The advocate was not examined as a witness.

value: On the afternoon of 8 September 1992, the victim went to a riverside ghat to bathe, accompanied by his son and his brother. Near the ghat, a group of men approached from the direction of a park. According to the eyewitness accounts, the group included the accused, who was carrying a country-made pistol, and other persons armed with a danda, kanta and knives. The group confronted the victim, caught hold of him and assaulted him with kanta and knives. On hearing his cries for help, the victim's son, another witness and the victim's brother ran towards the spot. As they approached, the accused fired a shot into the air from the pistol, after which the group fled from the scene through the south-western side. The victim was found dead on the steps of the ghat with his body partly in the water. A post-mortem examination recorded multiple incised and stab wounds on the head, face, neck, chest, back and arm, and the doctor opined that death was possibly caused by shock and haemorrhage from sharp-edged weapons. A written report was lodged at the police station shortly after the incident, and the investigating officers recorded statements of witnesses. Prior litigation between the families over property formed the background to the incident. No country-made pistol or cartridge was recovered from the scene.

value: On the night of 13 November 2011, at about 9.30 p.m., the victim and his mother were sleeping at their house in a village in Dewas district. Someone called the victim's name from outside and the victim opened the door. The victim's mother testified that she heard a gunshot and ran towards him. A second shot then struck the victim in the chest and he fell. Going outside, the mother saw the victim's wife and son standing on the opposite side of the house. She also saw two individuals with covered faces fleeing on a motorcycle. A country-made pistol was later recovered from the accused. A ballistic report found that the bullet recovered from the victim's body had been fired from that pistol. The prosecution case was that the location of the pistol was disclosed by a co-accused, who has since died, and that this disclosure led to the recovery of the pistol and to the arrest of the accused. No eyewitness identified the accused as a participant in the shooting. The case against the accused rested on the recovery of the pistol and the ballistic report. A First Information Report was registered on 13 November 2011, and a chargesheet was filed against several persons.
